In the event that this initiative measure and another
measure or measures pertaining to the review or
approval of essential projects, as defined in this act,
shall appear on the same statewide election ballot, the
other measure or measures shall be deemed to be in
conflict with this measure. In the event that this
initiative measure receives a greater number of
affirmative votes, the provisions of this measure shall
prevail in their entirety, and the provisions of the other
measure or measures shall be null and void.
SEC. 3. Liberal Construction.
This act shall be liberally construed to give effect to its
intent and purposes.
SEC. 4. Legal Defense.
The purpose of this section is to ensure that the
people’s precious right of initiative cannot be
improperly annulled by state politicians who refuse to
defend the will of the voters. Therefore, if this act is
approved by the voters of the State of California and
thereafter subjected to a legal challenge that
attempts to limit the scope or application of this act
in any way, or alleges this act violates any state or
federal law in whole or in part, and both the Governor
and Attorney General refuse to defend this act to the
fullest extent possible on behalf of the State of
California, then the following actions shall be taken:
(a) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary
contained in Chapter 6 (commencing with Section
12500) of Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the
Government Code or any other law, the Attorney
General shall appoint independent counsel to
faithfully and vigorously defend this act to the fullest
extent possible on behalf of the State of California.
(b) Before appointing or substituting independent
counsel, the Attorney General shall exercise due
diligence in determining the qualifications of
independent counsel and shall obtain written
affirmation from independent counsel that
independent counsel will faithfully and vigorously
defend this act to the fullest extent possible. The
written affirmation shall be made publicly available
immediately upon request.
(c) In order to support the defense of this act in
instances where the Governor and Attorney General
fail to do so despite the will of the voters, a continuous
appropriation is hereby made from the General Fund
to the Controller, without regard to fiscal years, in an
amount necessary to cover the costs of retaining
independent counsel to faithfully and vigorously
defend this act on behalf of the State of California to
the fullest extent possible.

General Provisions
21029. Construction of Chapter
(a) It is the policy of the people of the State of California
that this chapter be interpreted and implemented to
afford the fullest possible weight to the interest of, and
the approval and realization of, essential projects.
(b) (1) It is the intent of the people of the State of

accepted rules of statutory interpretation, not interpret
this division or the state CEQA Guidelines in a manner
that imposes procedural or substantive requirements
upon essential projects beyond those explicitly stated in
this division or the state CEQA Guidelines.

California that this subdivision be interpreted and
applied by the courts as directed by Section 21083.1,
and is in pari materia with Section 21083.1 so that, to
the maximum extent permitted under the law, this
subdivision constrains the authority of the courts to
issue a judgment or impose a remedy that is not
expressly authorized by this chapter.
21030. Statewide Concern
The people of the State of California hereby declare that
streamlining review and approval of essential projects
as provided in this chapter is a matter of statewide
concern because the adequacy, availability, and
affordability of housing, clean energy, water,
transportation, broadband internet, education facilities,
public health infrastructure, and public safety
infrastructure is insufficient to serve the needs of
California’s population and economy. Therefore, the
State of California hereby occupies the field in the area
of review and approval of essential projects as provided
in this chapter.

to state statutes or regulations codified outside of this
chapter refer to those statutes and regulations as they
existed on December 31, 2025, regardless of any
subsequent amendment, repeal, sunset, or expiration
that takes place after that date.

The provisions of this chapter are severable. If any
portion, section, subdivision, paragraph, subparagraph,
clause, subclause, sentence, phrase, word, or
application of this chapter is for any reason held to be
invalid by a decision of any court of competent
jurisdiction, that decision shall not affect the validity of
the remaining portions of this chapter. The people of the
State of California hereby declare that they would have
adopted this chapter and each and every portion,
section, subdivision, paragraph, subparagraph, clause,
subclause, sentence, phrase, word, and application not
declared invalid or unconstitutional without regard to

whether any component of this chapter or application
thereof would be subsequently declared invalid.

This chapter shall take effect as provided in subdivision
(a) of Section 10 of Article II of the California
Constitution, and shall be applicable upon that effective
date to all pending and future public agency and judicial
review and processes for all essential projects.
21034. Amendments
The Legislature may amend this chapter by a statute
passed in each house of the Legislature by rollcall vote
entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership
concurring, provided that the statute is consistent with,
and furthers the purposes of, this chapter. No bill
seeking to amend this chapter may be passed or
become a statute unless the bill has been printed and
distributed to the Members of the Legislature, and
published on the internet, in its final form, for at least
12 business days before its passage in either house of
the Legislature.
SEC. 2. Conflicting Measures.
In the event that this initiative measure and another
measure or measures pertaining to the review or
approval of essential projects, as defined in this act,
shall appear on the same statewide election ballot, the
other measure or measures shall be deemed to be in
conflict with this measure. In the event that this
initiative measure receives a greater number of
affirmative votes, the provisions of this measure shall
prevail in their entirety, and the provisions of the other
measure or measures shall be null and void.
SEC. 3. Liberal Construction.
This act shall be liberally construed to give effect to its
intent and purposes.
SEC. 4. Legal Defense.
The purpose of this section is to ensure that the
people’s precious right of initiative cannot be
improperly annulled by state politicians who refuse to
defend the will of the voters. Therefore, if this act is
approved by the voters of the State of California and
thereafter subjected to a legal challenge that
attempts to limit the scope or application of this act
in any way, or alleges this act violates any state or
federal law in whole or in part, and both the Governor
and Attorney General refuse to defend this act to the
fullest extent possible on behalf of the State of
California, then the following actions shall be taken:
(a) Notwithstanding anything to the contrary
contained in Chapter 6 (commencing with Section
12500) of Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the
Government Code or any other law, the Attorney
General shall appoint independent counsel to
faithfully and vigorously defend this act to the fullest
extent possible on behalf of the State of California.
(b) Before appointing or substituting independent
counsel, the Attorney General shall exercise due
diligence in determining the qualifications of
independent counsel and shall obtain written
affirmation from independent counsel that
independent counsel will faithfully and vigorously
defend this act to the fullest extent possible. The
written affirmation shall be made publicly available
immediately upon request.
(c) In order to support the defense of this act in

appropriation is hereby made from the General Fund
to the Controller, without regard to fiscal years, in an
amount necessary to cover the costs of retaining
independent counsel to faithfully and vigorously
defend this act on behalf of the State of California to
the fullest extent possible.

1. **Vested rights / "existing laws"**: Impacts assessed based on laws/standards in effect when application was submitted (Sec 21022(a), definition of "existing laws" at 21028(r)). Notable exception: life-safety standards and Building Code updates. This effectively freezes environmental standards for pending projects — a major concern raised by Biber.

2. **Applicant develops only ONE alternative** (Sec 21025), plus the no-project alternative. Also, "A proposed alternative developed pursuant to this article shall be presumed to lessen impacts... as long as the applicant demonstrates that substantial evidence exists to support the presumption." And agencies cannot require analysis of other alternatives.

3. **Public comment periods capped** at 20 days (negative declaration) / 45 days (draft EIR), can't be extended except by a court, and comments outside those windows "shall be disregarded and excluded from the administrative record." Notably: "significant changes to the essential project shall not include any changes to an essential project made in response to public comment" — meaning if the project changes in response to comments, no new comment period.

4. **Judicial review narrowed**: Claims limited to "noncompliance with objective existing laws" where "objective" means "involving no personal or subjective judgment and being uniformly verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark or criterion available and knowable... before the application was submitted." This is a huge narrowing — many CEQA standards (e.g., "significant effect on the environment," aesthetic impacts, biological impacts) are judgment-based, not "uniformly verifiable."

5. **Remedies narrowed**: Court can only prohibit the noncomplying part/phase/activity; cannot rescind approval. Injunctive relief only upon "clear and convincing evidence" of a "specific, adverse impact upon public safety" — a very high bar, and only for public safety (not environmental harm per se). Also, parts of a project not within the scope of the deficiency "not subject to further challenge." And "No further action or proceeding to challenge the implementation through completion of construction or subsequent approval" if approval wasn't challenged or was upheld.

6. **Statute of limitations**: 30 days from notice of determination to file; 270 days to resolve including appeals.

7. **"Fullest possible weight"** to approval and realization of essential projects (21029(a)); courts constrained from imposing requirements/remedies not expressly authorized.

8. **Preemption / occupies the field** (21030) — "the State of California hereby occupies the field in the area of review and approval of essential projects as provided in this chapter." Plus chapter controls over any conflicting law (21014(e)).

9. **Statutory references frozen as of Dec 31, 2025** (21031) — cross-references don't update with later amendments/repeals. This is a drafting landmine: as laws change, the frozen references become stale.

10. **Two-thirds legislative vote to amend**, and only if consistent with/furthering the chapter's purposes (21034). Hard lock-in.

11. **Conflicting measures clause** (SEC 2) — aggressive: any other measure "pertaining to the review or approval of essential projects" on the same ballot is deemed in conflict, and if Prop 45 gets more affirmative votes, the other measure is "null and void." Note this is unusual — normally conflicts are resolved only for provisions in conflict, and only if the measures are actually in conflict. This could nullify other voter-approved measures. (Check whether there are other measures on the 2026 ballot pertaining to review/approval of essential projects... probably not, but this is a risky clause.)

12. **Tribal consultation** limited to federally recognized tribes ("consulting tribe" definition), overriding "California Native American tribe" as used in AB 52-related sections. LA Times reported this sidelines dozens of tribes (California has ~110 federally recognized tribes but many more state-recognized/unrecognized tribes — roughly 100+ non-federally recognized).

13. **Labor standards**: Prevailing wage/union requirements apply for most essential projects (Section 21183.5 labor requirements) — for housing, prevailing wage applies only to buildings over 85 feet. So labor protections are partly preserved (which unions split over — California Labor Federation opposes).

14. **Applicants get new rights to sue agencies** over denials or "unlawful conditions of approval" (21020(g), 21023(g)) — a shift toward more litigation by developers, potentially.

15. Exclusions: jails/detention, new oil & gas production, Delta conveyance, high-speed rail, nuclear power. But "essential project" includes "all related and ancillary public, private, and utility infrastructure" — broad.

16. Broadband internet access project definition — data center ambiguity. Definition: "a project to provide massmarket retail service by wire service, wireless service, or radio to customers in this state that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all internet endpoints, including, but not limited to, any capabilities that are incidental to and enable the operation of the communications service." Independent legal experts divided; Data Center Coalition says data centers not eligible. But "all related and ancillary... infrastructure" could be read broadly. Also note "including... any capabilities that are incidental to and enable the operation of the communications service" is arguably expansive.

Also note: the mixed-use development definition excludes heavy industrial, extractive, port, refinery, hazardous materials uses — some protection.

Also, "essential housing project" includes "a subdivision or common interest development... consisting of residential units or unimproved residential lots" — i.e., greenfield sprawl subdivisions. That's the sprawl concern.

Now let me check a few more things:
- CalMatters voter guide recommendation (they have a 2026 voter guide).
- League of Women Voters position.
- The "No" side's argument about "no requirement that savings pass through" — verified: no affordability mandate in text.
- The "Yes" side claim: $75,000 per home savings — this figure comes from a 2023 study by the California Council for Affordable Housing/Holland & Knight? Let me verify. There's a study cited: "Research shows that permitting delays alone add tens of thousands of dollars to the price of a new home." The $75,000 figure is from the National Association of Home Builders (2022?) Actually NAHB says regulation accounts for 23.8% of the price of a new single-family home (~$85,000). The Holland & Knight study (Hernandez 2026 CEQA study) is cited.
- Key claim to check: whether most urban infill housing is already exempt via AB 130 (2025). CalMatters says AB 130 exempted most infill housing from CEQA, and 17,913 units entitled since. That weakens the housing-cost argument for Prop 45 — though it doesn't apply to projects >20 acres, and CEQA lawsuits can still be filed.
- Also check: does Prop 45 apply to logging? Biber said "Logging in general probably does." Hmm — under wildfire risk reduction project: "an activity that reduces wildfire risks to a residential or commercial structure" including vegetation management, fuel reduction... So commercial logging could qualify as "wildfire risk reduction" if framed that way. That's a real concern.
- Check: "essential clean energy project" includes carbon capture and storage, hydrogen — could include fossil-fuel-adjacent projects (though hydrogen must be non-fossil-derived).
- Note also: Prop 45 applies to public agencies' own projects too, which cuts both ways.

Let me also check the CalMatters voter guide recommendation, the League of Women Voters, and see if there's any "pro-housing progressive" case for Yes (e.g., Abundant Housing LA neutral, SPUR neutral). Also check whether there's an alternate, better-targeted reform option (e.g., legislative) — the SF Chronicle argued the Legislature is the better venue; Newsom vetoed a CEQA reform bill? Let's check the SacBee article "After Newsom veto, CEQA fight moves from the Capitol to the ballot box."

Let me also check whether Prop 45's "Yes" campaign made any commitments about affordability, and whether any notable progressive/pro-housing voices endorse Yes (Buffy Wicks does).

Also check money: $56M yes vs $30M no; top contributors.

Powerful Interests Aim to Weaken California’s Landmark Environmental Law
Utilities, developers and technology companies have spent tens of millions to pass Prop 45, which fast-tracks “essential” projects by limiting public and environmental review.
By Liza Gross (https://insideclimatenews.org/profile/liza-gross/)
October 28, 2026

Political action committees funded by technology companies, the state’s major utilities and other corporate interests have spent several million dollars more to pass a ballot measure that would greenlight major development projects with minimal environmental or public review than public interest and labor groups have spent opposing it.
Developers and other corporate interests aim to streamline the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA (https://www.califaep.org/docs/CEQA_Handbook_2023_final.pdf), which requires public agencies to identify, disclose and mitigate a development project’s negative impacts on a wide range of environmental resources, including wildlife, air and water quality and tribal cultural resources.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf) shifts who determines the scope of environmental review from public agencies and communities to project developers by rewriting the state’s foundational environmental law to fast-track major projects.
Supporters of Prop 45, sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, have spent at least $36 million to pass the measure, the most recent state records show. Opponents, led by a coalition of more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations, have spent about $30 million to defeat what they say will give polluters a free pass.

“Prop 45 will modernize the approval process for essential projects by establishing clear, enforceable timelines for agency decisions and court challenges,” the chamber said in promotional materials, “while keeping environmental protections intact and preserving worker protections, tribal protections and local control.”
Critics say Prop 45 will gut the state’s primary vehicle for allowing people to learn about plans for polluting developments in their neighborhoods and propose alternatives.
“It undermines basically every stage of that process,” said Woody Little, the spokesperson for No on Prop 45.
Little and his allies say the 41-page ballot measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) was written by corporations who have paid to get their special interests on the ballot to create loopholes that favor polluting industries like recently regulated (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/21/governor-newsom-signs-most-comprehensive-data-center-laws-in-the-nation-providing-communities-more-control-on-water-electricity-and-land-use/) data centers while limiting the input of communities and local tribes.
Critics of CEQA, signed in 1970 by then-Gov. Ronald Reagan, blame the law for hobbling home construction and driving housing and cost of living increases in California, which are among the highest in the nation.
Prop 45 will lower housing and utility costs by reducing “endless” bureaucratic delays and protect taxpayers by reducing waste and cost overruns, Yes on Prop 45 materials argue.
Yet there is no requirement in the measure to reduce housing costs or utility bills. And the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) estimates that Prop 45 could leave state and local governments paying $100 million or more a year, partly to cover fast-tracked projects’ environmental impacts.
“The housing issue is a smokescreen for all these other polluting projects,” said Little.
California passed laws last year that significantly streamlined CEQA by exempting (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB130) urban and mixed-use housing construction from its provisions as well as certain infrastructure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB131) and clean energy (https://www.energy.ca.gov/programs-and-topics/topics/power-plants/opt-certification-program) projects.
“ I would hope that 100 percent of Californians would see this radical reshaping of California’s environmental law for the dangerous thing that it is. A wolf in sheep’s clothing.”
— Woody Little, No on Prop 45
None of the grassroots groups that promote “yes in my backyard,” or YIMBY (https://yimbyaction.org/), policies to build more housing and public transit in urban and suburban areas support Prop 45, Little said. Most are neutral, he said, while others oppose it.
Expanding housing beyond already developed areas means building new freeways, water connections and other expensive infrastructure that taxpayers ultimately pay for, Little said. And these projects often encroach on the wildland-urban interface, raising wildfire risk just as climate change is making fires more destructive.
At a time when California is already seeing the catastrophic costs of climate-fueled fires, Little said, the state should be requiring more environmental review around developments to assess and mitigate risk, not less.
What’s “Essential”?
Prop 45 covers nine types of “essential” projects, among them housing, water systems, clean energy (including carbon capture and storage), transportation, wildfire risk reduction and broadband internet access. All related and “ancillary” infrastructure is also covered.
Whether “ancillary” includes data centers, which typically require broadband infrastructure (https://tiaonline.org/how-broadband-workforce-development-and-standards-drive-data-center-growth/), has been a major point of contention.
Prop 45’s proponents have insisted the measure does not cover data centers, but legal experts disagree, pointing to $2 million in donations from just three data center builders and language buried in the measure’s 41 pages. Eligible projects include “broadband internet access projects,” defined as “mass-market retail service … that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all Internet endpoints,” a recent analysis (https://www.dailyjournal.com/articles/394431-prop-45-will-speed-data-center-construction) found.

That definition includes facilities that house the physical infrastructure used to transmit consumer data to and from the internet—which describes many data centers.
Yet data centers are conspicuously absent from the list of excluded controversial projects, which includes high-speed rail, the Delta Conveyance Project (https://www.deltaconveyanceproject.com/about-the-delta-conveyance-project), nuclear power and oil and gas facilities.
Inside Climate News asked the Yes on Prop 45 campaign why it sought to further limit environmental review after California had already significantly streamlined CEQA and why the measure does not explicitly exclude data centers. The campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
California Resources Corp., the state’s largest (https://www.crc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/california-resources-corporation-completes-acquisition-crimson) oil and gas producer, has donated $500,000 directly to Prop 45 campaigns and another $500,000 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1021742&session=2025&view=received) to a business committee sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce. Oil and gas facilities are explicitly excluded from Prop 45, but CRC has a data center under environmental review at its Elk Hills oil field.
CRC did not respond to questions about whether it supports Prop 45 in order to fast-track its data center application.
Protecting Community Voices
“Proposition 45 would weaken CEQA protections for the very projects that still warrant careful scrutiny—development that could put people in harm’s way, fragment wildlife habitat, threaten water resources or damage irreplaceable cultural and sacred sites,” environmental and conservation leaders argued in a recent op-ed (https://lookout.co/california-has-already-streamlined-ceqa-proposition-45-goes-too-far/story).
One of the op-ed authors, Chris Wilmers, tracks mountain lions as lead researcher for the Santa Cruz Puma Project. In his study area, retaliatory killings for preying on domestic animals and vehicle strikes are the biggest threat (https://lookout.co/mountain-lions-ucsc-researcher-chris-wilmers-on-how-new-highway-17-animal-crossing-protects-santa-cruz-mountain-lions/story) to mountain lions as new housing and roads continue to encroach on the wide-ranging carnivores’ critical habitat.
An adult male mountain lion travels through a tunnel under Highway 101, heading south toward California’s Santa Monica Mountains in 2018. Credit: National Parks Service
CEQA requires developers to weigh alternatives to mitigate harm if new evidence emerges that a project would degrade critical wildlife corridors or endangered species’ habitat. But such facts would never come to light under Prop 45, which lets developers write their own rules, Wilmers and others say.
And the ballot measure strips away the rights of tribes that aren’t recognized by the federal government to safeguard their sacred lands.
That leaves large swaths of California, including the Central Coast, the San Francisco Bay Area and much of the Los Angeles area, without any tribal representation, said Noelle Chambers, executive director of the Amah Mutsun Land Trust.
Ethnographic studies conducted through CEQA consultations allowed the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band to protect burial grounds, artifacts and other sacred sites by stopping a proposed sand and gravel mine (https://openspacetrust.org/blog/sargent-ranch/) near Gilroy.
Prop 45 creates a “really harmful” legal precedent in the state by excluding non-federally recognized tribes from the process, Chambers said.
Julia Stein, deputy director of the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the University of California, Los Angeles, calls Prop 45 “a blunt force instrument” that is unlikely to build more projects faster by removing public participation.
It will cause a real loss of community engagement, she said, noting that CEQA is the only avenue for environmental justice communities to influence the environmental impacts of projects in their neighborhoods.
“We lived through a big infrastructure build-out in this country without laws like CEQA in the 1950s and ’60s, and we got environmental justice communities right next to freeways as a result,” Stein said.
CEQA has helped many communities (https://www.phi.org/thought-leadership/act-on-climate-california-communities-addressing-climate-change-and-health/) with elevated rates of asthma, cancer, heart disease and other ailments linked to industrial pollution limit additional harms in their neighborhoods.
A historically overburdened Latino community in southeast Los Angeles used a court order to compel a local government (https://legal-planet.org/2022/02/23/why-ceqa-is-a-useful-tool-for-environmental-justice-communities-in-california/) to review the risks of building an elementary school on a site contaminated with arsenic, and likely lead and asbestos, and require a cleanup. The mostly Latino residents of Riverside County’s Moreno Valley won an agreement to mitigate the harms (https://biologicaldiversity.org/programs/energy-justice/pdfs/WorldLogisticsCenter-Settlement-Agreement-20210429.pdf) on local air quality, climate and wildlife created by heavy-duty trucks serving a 40-million-square-foot warehouse.
Such mitigating measures might never have been identified, let alone required, if Prop 45 had been in effect, opponents say.
In addition to reducing the timeline for public agencies to review projects and fundamentally changing who can provide input, Prop 45 says only the developer or corporation can propose alternatives, said Mabel Tsang, political director for the California Environmental Justice Alliance, which opposes Prop 45.
“That takes away the strongest tool that communities like ours can use to protect ourselves from the worst health impacts before another polluting project is approved next door to our homes,” Tsang said.
Reagan, who signed CEQA as California governor but was known for accelerating deregulation as president, saw environmental protection as a nonpartisan issue. “Preservation of our environment is not a liberal or conservative challenge, it’s common sense,” he said during his 1984 State of the Union (https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/archives/speech/address-joint-session-congress-state-union-january-1984) address.
Now, on the heels of the Trump administration’s attempts to roll back the nation’s major environmental laws, experts say CEQA is more important than ever to safeguard public health and the environment from polluting industries.
Recent polling suggests that on Nov. 3, voters may not approve a measure designed to kneecap California’s most important air- and water-quality protection law.
A poll released Tuesday (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) by the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California shows that 50 percent of voters oppose Prop 45, while those who support it dropped to 46 percent from 73 percent in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), when voters knew only general information about the proposition.

Powerful Interests Aim to Weaken California’s Landmark Environmental Law
Utilities, developers and technology companies have spent tens of millions to pass Prop 45, which fast-tracks “essential” projects by limiting public and environmental review.
By Liza Gross (https://insideclimatenews.org/profile/liza-gross/)

Political action committees funded by technology companies, the state’s major utilities and other corporate interests have spent several million dollars more to pass a ballot measure that would greenlight major development projects with minimal environmental or public review than public interest and labor groups have spent opposing it.
Developers and other corporate interests aim to streamline the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA (https://www.califaep.org/docs/CEQA_Handbook_2023_final.pdf), which requires public agencies to identify, disclose and mitigate a development project’s negative impacts on a wide range of environmental resources, including wildlife, air and water quality and tribal cultural resources.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf) shifts who determines the scope of environmental review from public agencies and communities to project developers by rewriting the state’s foundational environmental law to fast-track major projects.
Supporters of Prop 45, sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, have spent at least $36 million to pass the measure, the most recent state records show. Opponents, led by a coalition of more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations, have spent about $30 million to defeat what they say will give polluters a free pass.

Political action committees funded by technology companies, the state’s major utilities and other corporate interests have spent several million dollars more to pass a ballot measure that would greenlight major development projects with minimal environmental or public review than public interest and labor groups have spent opposing it.
Developers and other corporate interests aim to streamline the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA (https://www.califaep.org/docs/CEQA_Handbook_2023_final.pdf), which requires public agencies to identify, disclose and mitigate a development project’s negative impacts on a wide range of environmental resources, including wildlife, air and water quality and tribal cultural resources.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf) shifts who determines the scope of environmental review from public agencies and communities to project developers by rewriting the state’s foundational environmental law to fast-track major projects.
Supporters of Prop 45, sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, have spent at least $36 million to pass the measure, the most recent state records show. Opponents, led by a coalition of more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations, have spent about $30 million to defeat what they say will give polluters a free pass.

Now I have a thorough picture of the text. Key provisions confirmed:

1. **Vested rights / "existing laws"**: Impacts assessed based on laws/standards in effect when application was submitted (Sec 21022(a), definition of "existing laws" at 21028(r)). Notable exception: life-safety standards and Building Code updates. This effectively freezes environmental standards for pending projects — a major concern raised by Biber.

2. **Applicant develops only ONE alternative** (Sec 21025), plus the no-project alternative. Also, "A proposed alternative developed pursuant to this article shall be presumed to lessen impacts... as long as the applicant demonstrates that substantial evidence exists to support the presumption." And agencies cannot require analysis of other alternatives.

3. **Public comment periods capped** at 20 days (negative declaration) / 45 days (draft EIR), can't be extended except by a court, and comments outside those windows "shall be disregarded and excluded from the administrative record." Notably: "significant changes to the essential project shall not include any changes to an essential project made in response to public comment" — meaning if the project changes in response to comments, no new comment period.

4. **Judicial review narrowed**: Claims limited to "noncompliance with objective existing laws" where "objective" means "involving no personal or subjective judgment and being uniformly verifiable by reference to an external and uniform benchmark or criterion available and knowable... before the application was submitted." This is a huge narrowing — many CEQA standards (e.g., "significant effect on the environment," aesthetic impacts, biological impacts) are judgment-based, not "uniformly verifiable."

5. **Remedies narrowed**: Court can only prohibit the noncomplying part/phase/activity; cannot rescind approval. Injunctive relief only upon "clear and convincing evidence" of a "specific, adverse impact upon public safety" — a very high bar, and only for public safety (not environmental harm per se). Also, parts of a project not within the scope of the deficiency "not subject to further challenge." And "No further action or proceeding to challenge the implementation through completion of construction or subsequent approval" if approval wasn't challenged or was upheld.

6. **Statute of limitations**: 30 days from notice of determination to file; 270 days to resolve including appeals.

7. **"Fullest possible weight"** to approval and realization of essential projects (21029(a)); courts constrained from imposing requirements/remedies not expressly authorized.

8. **Preemption / occupies the field** (21030) — "the State of California hereby occupies the field in the area of review and approval of essential projects as provided in this chapter." Plus chapter controls over any conflicting law (21014(e)).

9. **Statutory references frozen as of Dec 31, 2025** (21031) — cross-references don't update with later amendments/repeals. This is a drafting landmine: as laws change, the frozen references become stale.

10. **Two-thirds legislative vote to amend**, and only if consistent with/furthering the chapter's purposes (21034). Hard lock-in.

11. **Conflicting measures clause** (SEC 2) — aggressive: any other measure "pertaining to the review or approval of essential projects" on the same ballot is deemed in conflict, and if Prop 45 gets more affirmative votes, the other measure is "null and void." Note this is unusual — normally conflicts are resolved only for provisions in conflict, and only if the measures are actually in conflict. This could nullify other voter-approved measures. (Check whether there are other measures on the 2026 ballot pertaining to review/approval of essential projects... probably not, but this is a risky clause.)

12. **Tribal consultation** limited to federally recognized tribes ("consulting tribe" definition), overriding "California Native American tribe" as used in AB 52-related sections. LA Times reported this sidelines dozens of tribes (California has ~110 federally recognized tribes but many more state-recognized/unrecognized tribes — roughly 100+ non-federally recognized).

13. **Labor standards**: Prevailing wage/union requirements apply for most essential projects (Section 21183.5 labor requirements) — for housing, prevailing wage applies only to buildings over 85 feet. So labor protections are partly preserved (which unions split over — California Labor Federation opposes).

14. **Applicants get new rights to sue agencies** over denials or "unlawful conditions of approval" (21020(g), 21023(g)) — a shift toward more litigation by developers, potentially.

15. Exclusions: jails/detention, new oil & gas production, Delta conveyance, high-speed rail, nuclear power. But "essential project" includes "all related and ancillary public, private, and utility infrastructure" — broad.

16. Broadband internet access project definition — data center ambiguity. Definition: "a project to provide massmarket retail service by wire service, wireless service, or radio to customers in this state that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all internet endpoints, including, but not limited to, any capabilities that are incidental to and enable the operation of the communications service." Independent legal experts divided; Data Center Coalition says data centers not eligible. But "all related and ancillary... infrastructure" could be read broadly. Also note "including... any capabilities that are incidental to and enable the operation of the communications service" is arguably expansive.

Also note: the mixed-use development definition excludes heavy industrial, extractive, port, refinery, hazardous materials uses — some protection.

Also, "essential housing project" includes "a subdivision or common interest development... consisting of residential units or unimproved residential lots" — i.e., greenfield sprawl subdivisions. That's the sprawl concern.

Now let me check a few more things:
- CalMatters voter guide recommendation (they have a 2026 voter guide).
- League of Women Voters position.
- The "No" side's argument about "no requirement that savings pass through" — verified: no affordability mandate in text.
- The "Yes" side claim: $75,000 per home savings — this figure comes from a 2023 study by the California Council for Affordable Housing/Holland & Knight? Let me verify. There's a study cited: "Research shows that permitting delays alone add tens of thousands of dollars to the price of a new home." The $75,000 figure is from the National Association of Home Builders (2022?) Actually NAHB says regulation accounts for 23.8% of the price of a new single-family home (~$85,000). The Holland & Knight study (Hernandez 2026 CEQA study) is cited.
- Key claim to check: whether most urban infill housing is already exempt via AB 130 (2025). CalMatters says AB 130 exempted most infill housing from CEQA, and 17,913 units entitled since. That weakens the housing-cost argument for Prop 45 — though it doesn't apply to projects >20 acres, and CEQA lawsuits can still be filed.
- Also check: does Prop 45 apply to logging? Biber said "Logging in general probably does." Hmm — under wildfire risk reduction project: "an activity that reduces wildfire risks to a residential or commercial structure" including vegetation management, fuel reduction... So commercial logging could qualify as "wildfire risk reduction" if framed that way. That's a real concern.
- Check: "essential clean energy project" includes carbon capture and storage, hydrogen — could include fossil-fuel-adjacent projects (though hydrogen must be non-fossil-derived).
- Note also: Prop 45 applies to public agencies' own projects too, which cuts both ways.

Let me also check the CalMatters voter guide recommendation, the League of Women Voters, and see if there's any "pro-housing progressive" case for Yes (e.g., Abundant Housing LA neutral, SPUR neutral). Also check whether there's an alternate, better-targeted reform option (e.g., legislative) — the SF Chronicle argued the Legislature is the better venue; Newsom vetoed a CEQA reform bill? Let's check the SacBee article "After Newsom veto, CEQA fight moves from the Capitol to the ballot box."

Let me also check whether Prop 45's "Yes" campaign made any commitments about affordability, and whether any notable progressive/pro-housing voices endorse Yes (Buffy Wicks does).

Also check money: $56M yes vs $30M no; top contributors.

Let me search for these.

Political action committees funded by technology companies, the state’s major utilities and other corporate interests have spent several million dollars more to pass a ballot measure that would greenlight major development projects with minimal environmental or public review than public interest and labor groups have spent opposing it.
Developers and other corporate interests aim to streamline the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA (https://www.califaep.org/docs/CEQA_Handbook_2023_final.pdf), which requires public agencies to identify, disclose and mitigate a development project’s negative impacts on a wide range of environmental resources, including wildlife, air and water quality and tribal cultural resources.
Proposition 45 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop45-text-proposed-laws.pdf) shifts who determines the scope of environmental review from public agencies and communities to project developers by rewriting the state’s foundational environmental law to fast-track major projects.
Supporters of Prop 45, sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, have spent at least $36 million to pass the measure, the most recent state records show. Opponents, led by a coalition of more than 550 labor, health and environmental organizations, have spent about $30 million to defeat what they say will give polluters a free pass.

“Prop 45 will modernize the approval process for essential projects by establishing clear, enforceable timelines for agency decisions and court challenges,” the chamber said in promotional materials, “while keeping environmental protections intact and preserving worker protections, tribal protections and local control.”
Critics say Prop 45 will gut the state’s primary vehicle for allowing people to learn about plans for polluting developments in their neighborhoods and propose alternatives.
“It undermines basically every stage of that process,” said Woody Little, the spokesperson for No on Prop 45.
Little and his allies say the 41-page ballot measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) was written by corporations who have paid to get their special interests on the ballot to create loopholes that favor polluting industries like recently regulated (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/21/governor-newsom-signs-most-comprehensive-data-center-laws-in-the-nation-providing-communities-more-control-on-water-electricity-and-land-use/) data centers while limiting the input of communities and local tribes.
Critics of CEQA, signed in 1970 by then-Gov. Ronald Reagan, blame the law for hobbling home construction and driving housing and cost of living increases in California, which are among the highest in the nation.
Prop 45 will lower housing and utility costs by reducing “endless” bureaucratic delays and protect taxpayers by reducing waste and cost overruns, Yes on Prop 45 materials argue.
Yet there is no requirement in the measure to reduce housing costs or utility bills. And the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) estimates that Prop 45 could leave state and local governments paying $100 million or more a year, partly to cover fast-tracked projects’ environmental impacts.
“The housing issue is a smokescreen for all these other polluting projects,” said Little.
California passed laws last year that significantly streamlined CEQA by exempting (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB130) urban and mixed-use housing construction from its provisions as well as certain infrastructure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB131) and clean energy (https://www.energy.ca.gov/programs-and-topics/topics/power-plants/opt-certification-program) projects.
“ I would hope that 100 percent of Californians would see this radical reshaping of California’s environmental law for the dangerous thing that it is. A wolf in sheep’s clothing.”
— Woody Little, No on Prop 45
None of the grassroots groups that promote “yes in my backyard,” or YIMBY (https://yimbyaction.org/), policies to build more housing and public transit in urban and suburban areas support Prop 45, Little said. Most are neutral, he said, while others oppose it.
Expanding housing beyond already developed areas means building new freeways, water connections and other expensive infrastructure that taxpayers ultimately pay for, Little said. And these projects often encroach on the wildland-urban interface, raising wildfire risk just as climate change is making fires more destructive.
At a time when California is already seeing the catastrophic costs of climate-fueled fires, Little said, the state should be requiring more environmental review around developments to assess and mitigate risk, not less.
What’s “Essential”?
Prop 45 covers nine types of “essential” projects, among them housing, water systems, clean energy (including carbon capture and storage), transportation, wildfire risk reduction and broadband internet access. All related and “ancillary” infrastructure is also covered.
Whether “ancillary” includes data centers, which typically require broadband infrastructure (https://tiaonline.org/how-broadband-workforce-development-and-standards-drive-data-center-growth/), has been a major point of contention.
Prop 45’s proponents have insisted the measure does not cover data centers, but legal experts disagree, pointing to $2 million in donations from just three data center builders and language buried in the measure’s 41 pages. Eligible projects include “broadband internet access projects,” defined as “mass-market retail service … that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all Internet endpoints,” a recent analysis (https://www.dailyjournal.com/articles/394431-prop-45-will-speed-data-center-construction) found.

That definition includes facilities that house the physical infrastructure used to transmit consumer data to and from the internet—which describes many data centers.
Yet data centers are conspicuously absent from the list of excluded controversial projects, which includes high-speed rail, the Delta Conveyance Project (https://www.deltaconveyanceproject.com/about-the-delta-conveyance-project), nuclear power and oil and gas facilities.
Inside Climate News asked the Yes on Prop 45 campaign why it sought to further limit environmental review after California had already significantly streamlined CEQA and why the measure does not explicitly exclude data centers. The campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
California Resources Corp., the state’s largest (https://www.crc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/california-resources-corporation-completes-acquisition-crimson) oil and gas producer, has donated $500,000 directly to Prop 45 campaigns and another $500,000 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1021742&session=2025&view=received) to a business committee sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce. Oil and gas facilities are explicitly excluded from Prop 45, but CRC has a data center under environmental review at its Elk Hills oil field.
CRC did not respond to questions about whether it supports Prop 45 in order to fast-track its data center application.
Protecting Community Voices
“Proposition 45 would weaken CEQA protections for the very projects that still warrant careful scrutiny—development that could put people in harm’s way, fragment wildlife habitat, threaten water resources or damage irreplaceable cultural and sacred sites,” environmental and conservation leaders argued in a recent op-ed (https://lookout.co/california-has-already-streamlined-ceqa-proposition-45-goes-too-far/story).
One of the op-ed authors, Chris Wilmers, tracks mountain lions as lead researcher for the Santa Cruz Puma Project. In his study area, retaliatory killings for preying on domestic animals and vehicle strikes are the biggest threat (https://lookout.co/mountain-lions-ucsc-researcher-chris-wilmers-on-how-new-highway-17-animal-crossing-protects-santa-cruz-mountain-lions/story) to mountain lions as new housing and roads continue to encroach on the wide-ranging carnivores’ critical habitat.
An adult male mountain lion travels through a tunnel under Highway 101, heading south toward California’s Santa Monica Mountains in 2018. Credit: National Parks Service
CEQA requires developers to weigh alternatives to mitigate harm if new evidence emerges that a project would degrade critical wildlife corridors or endangered species’ habitat. But such facts would never come to light under Prop 45, which lets developers write their own rules, Wilmers and others say.
And the ballot measure strips away the rights of tribes that aren’t recognized by the federal government to safeguard their sacred lands.
That leaves large swaths of California, including the Central Coast, the San Francisco Bay Area and much of the Los Angeles area, without any tribal representation, said Noelle Chambers, executive director of the Amah Mutsun Land Trust.
Ethnographic studies conducted through CEQA consultations allowed the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band to protect burial grounds, artifacts and other sacred sites by stopping a proposed sand and gravel mine (https://openspacetrust.org/blog/sargent-ranch/) near Gilroy.
Prop 45 creates a “really harmful” legal precedent in the state by excluding non-federally recognized tribes from the process, Chambers said.
Julia Stein, deputy director of the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the University of California, Los Angeles, calls Prop 45 “a blunt force instrument” that is unlikely to build more projects faster by removing public participation.
It will cause a real loss of community engagement, she said, noting that CEQA is the only avenue for environmental justice communities to influence the environmental impacts of projects in their neighborhoods.
“We lived through a big infrastructure build-out in this country without laws like CEQA in the 1950s and ’60s, and we got environmental justice communities right next to freeways as a result,” Stein said.
CEQA has helped many communities (https://www.phi.org/thought-leadership/act-on-climate-california-communities-addressing-climate-change-and-health/) with elevated rates of asthma, cancer, heart disease and other ailments linked to industrial pollution limit additional harms in their neighborhoods.
A historically overburdened Latino community in southeast Los Angeles used a court order to compel a local government (https://legal-planet.org/2022/02/23/why-ceqa-is-a-useful-tool-for-environmental-justice-communities-in-california/) to review the risks of building an elementary school on a site contaminated with arsenic, and likely lead and asbestos, and require a cleanup. The mostly Latino residents of Riverside County’s Moreno Valley won an agreement to mitigate the harms (https://biologicaldiversity.org/programs/energy-justice/pdfs/WorldLogisticsCenter-Settlement-Agreement-20210429.pdf) on local air quality, climate and wildlife created by heavy-duty trucks serving a 40-million-square-foot warehouse.
Such mitigating measures might never have been identified, let alone required, if Prop 45 had been in effect, opponents say.
In addition to reducing the timeline for public agencies to review projects and fundamentally changing who can provide input, Prop 45 says only the developer or corporation can propose alternatives, said Mabel Tsang, political director for the California Environmental Justice Alliance, which opposes Prop 45.
“That takes away the strongest tool that communities like ours can use to protect ourselves from the worst health impacts before another polluting project is approved next door to our homes,” Tsang said.
Reagan, who signed CEQA as California governor but was known for accelerating deregulation as president, saw environmental protection as a nonpartisan issue. “Preservation of our environment is not a liberal or conservative challenge, it’s common sense,” he said during his 1984 State of the Union (https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/archives/speech/address-joint-session-congress-state-union-january-1984) address.
Now, on the heels of the Trump administration’s attempts to roll back the nation’s major environmental laws, experts say CEQA is more important than ever to safeguard public health and the environment from polluting industries.
Recent polling suggests that on Nov. 3, voters may not approve a measure designed to kneecap California’s most important air- and water-quality protection law.
A poll released Tuesday (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) by the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California shows that 50 percent of voters oppose Prop 45, while those who support it dropped to 46 percent from 73 percent in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), when voters knew only general information about the proposition.

Proposition 45
Speed up environmental reviews for housing and infrastructure
Proposition 45 would limit reviews under the state’s landmark environmental law, the California Environmental Quality Act. Placed on the ballot by the California Chamber of Commerce, the measure aims to help developers advance projects they designate as “essential” more quickly and easily. It would impose a 365-day limit on environmental reviews for those projects, including infrastructure like roads and bridges, housing, schools, broadband and wildfire mitigation. It would also require courts to rule within 270 days on lawsuits related to the environmental review law.

Summary
Support
The California Chamber of Commerce says the state’s environmental review law is outdated and creates expensive bureaucracy and frivolous litigation that slows development. It argues that delays in reviewing projects ultimately increase costs that are passed down to taxpayers and consumers. The group argues the measure will speed up development while keeping essential environmental protections in place.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure would weaken California’s environmental review law, which exists to protect people and the environment from potentially harmful developments. They say Proposition 45 would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate their ability to enforce the law. They argue the long-term costs of poor planning will be passed onto agencies and taxpayers.

MODIFIES ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW FOR CERTAIN PROJECTS. INITIATIVE STATUTE. Proposition 45
Speed up environmental reviews for housing and infrastructure
Proposition 45 would limit reviews under the state’s landmark environmental law, the California Environmental Quality Act. Placed on the ballot by the California Chamber of Commerce, the measure aims to help developers advance projects they designate as “essential” more quickly and easily. It would impose a 365-day limit on environmental reviews for those projects, including infrastructure like roads and bridges, housing, schools, broadband and wildfire mitigation. It would also require courts to rule within 270 days on lawsuits related to the environmental review law.

Summary
Support
The California Chamber of Commerce says the state’s environmental review law is outdated and creates expensive bureaucracy and frivolous litigation that slows development. It argues that delays in reviewing projects ultimately increase costs that are passed down to taxpayers and consumers. The group argues the measure will speed up development while keeping essential environmental protections in place.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure would weaken California’s environmental review law, which exists to protect people and the environment from potentially harmful developments. They say Proposition 45 would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate their ability to enforce the law. They argue the long-term costs of poor planning will be passed onto agencies and taxpayers.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Fiscal Impact: Initial costs for state and local governments, likely in the high tens of millions of dollars potentially exceeding $100 million–annually, partly covered by fees. Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects.

Proposition 45
Speed up environmental reviews for housing and infrastructure
Proposition 45 would limit reviews under the state’s landmark environmental law, the California Environmental Quality Act. Placed on the ballot by the California Chamber of Commerce, the measure aims to help developers advance projects they designate as “essential” more quickly and easily. It would impose a 365-day limit on environmental reviews for those projects, including infrastructure like roads and bridges, housing, schools, broadband and wildfire mitigation. It would also require courts to rule within 270 days on lawsuits related to the environmental review law.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.

Support
Oppose
Summary
Support
The California Chamber of Commerce says the state’s environmental review law is outdated and creates expensive bureaucracy and frivolous litigation that slows development. It argues that delays in reviewing projects ultimately increase costs that are passed down to taxpayers and consumers. The group argues the measure will speed up development while keeping essential environmental protections in place.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure would weaken California’s environmental review law, which exists to protect people and the environment from potentially harmful developments. They say Proposition 45 would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate their ability to enforce the law. They argue the long-term costs of poor planning will be passed onto agencies and taxpayers.

### Additional Titles

### Summary
Proposition 45 began as initiative 25-0023, filed by proponent Kurt Oneto with the California Attorney General’s Office on October 21, 2025.

Proposition 45 creates a new review process for certain projects defined as “essential.”

### Background
***People Can Sue the Government Agency About Its CEQA Review.*** After a government agency has completed the CEQA review and decided whether to approve a project, people who think the agency did not follow the CEQA process correctly can sue the agency.
For example, a project opponent might argue that the environmental analysis was inadequate.
If the court finds that the agency did not follow CEQA correctly, it can stop the whole project and require the agency to fix the part of the process that was problematic.

Proposition 45 creates new procedures for reviewing certain types of projects that it defines as “essential.”

SACRAMENTO, Calif.

Gavin Newsom vetoed a bill last week to narrow an exemption to the California Environmental Quality Act for manufacturing facilities.
But the long-running political struggle over the cornerstone law continues apace, with both sides now turning their full attention from the Capitol to the voters.

Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney General title and summary, December 26, 2025)
Measure’s own name: The Building an Affordable California Act (AG No. 25-0023A1)
Type: Initiated state statute
A vote YES means: A new “essential projects” category (most housing, water, clean energy, medical, public safety, broadband, and transportation projects) gets hard deadlines for CEQA review, a slimmed-down alternatives analysis, and tighter limits on lawsuits, all written into the Public Resources Code [1, Sec. 21013].
A vote NO means: CEQA’s existing review timelines, alternatives requirements, and judicial-review rules stay in place for these projects.
Sponsor/proponent: California Chamber of Commerce. Proponent of record: Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer LLP.
On the ballot because: Qualified by random-sample signature check on June 16, 2026, and certified eligible June 25, 2026. The measure needed 546,651 valid signatures.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0023 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-023)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 45 would carve a new fast-track lane through the California Environmental Quality Act for what it calls “essential projects.” It adds a new chapter, Chapter 1.5, to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code, the part of state law that is CEQA. It does not repeal CEQA, and it does not touch the other environmental statutes it names, such as the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the California Coastal Act. What it changes is CEQA’s procedure for a defined set of projects [1, Sec. 1 (21011(h)), 21012-21033].
The measure does three main things for essential projects. First, it puts public agencies on a clock. An agency has thirty days to decide whether an application is complete or the application is deemed complete automatically. Once complete, a lead agency has 365 days to decide whether to certify an environmental impact report (EIR), 180 days to act on a negative declaration, and 90 days to document an exemption. For the 365-day and 90-day review clocks the measure counts only business days, not weekends or state holidays, so the real-world calendar is longer than the raw numbers suggest [1, Secs. 21017-21019, 21028(c)].
Second, it shrinks the alternatives analysis. Today a CEQA environmental impact report must study a reasonable range of alternatives to a project. Under Proposition 45, an EIR for an essential project needs to analyze only the project itself, one alternative developed by the applicant, and the “no project” alternative. The measure declares that any additional alternatives are “unnecessary” and that no agency may require them [1, Sec. 21025].
Third, it narrows the courtroom. A challenger must sue within thirty days of the agency’s notice of determination, the case must finish within 270 days including any appeal, and the court must use the deferential substantial-evidence standard rather than independent judgment. A court that finds a defect may order the agency to redo only the specific study at issue. It “may not order or direct” the agency to rescind its approval of the project, and once a project clears review its later construction and implementation approvals cannot be challenged again [1, Secs. 21026-21027].
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (amended language submitted November 24, 2025)
Key language:
“‘Essential project’ means a project that meets all of the following requirements … The project does not include a jail or other detention facility, or involve the development of a new oil or natural gas production facility.” [1, Sec. 21028(h)]
“A court may not order or direct via writ or any other form of order, injunction, or decision that an agency rescind its approval of the essential project.” [1, Sec. 21027(d)]
What it amends: Adds Chapter 1.5 (commencing with Section 21010) to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code. Because it is an initiative statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, but only in ways that further the measure’s purposes unless it says otherwise. The measure also adds a self-defense clause. If the governor and attorney general both decline to defend it in court, the attorney general must appoint independent counsel, funded by a continuous general fund appropriation [1, Secs. 21010, Section 4].
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, with the initiative filed by attorney Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer. Supporters include the California Building Industry Association, the California Hospital Association, NAACP California, and Pacific Gas and Electric. Opposition is led by environmental organizations, including Sierra Club California, the Planning and Conservation League, and CalBike.
What? Jails and detention facilities and new oil and gas production facilities are excluded, and by definition Delta conveyance and high-speed rail are left out of the water and transportation categories. [1, Secs. 21013, 21028].
Where? Statewide, applied to all public agencies and written into the Public Resources Code [1, Sec. 21014(d)].
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. It takes effect the day after the election if it passes and applies to applications deemed complete after that date, including projects that withdraw and resubmit to opt in [1, Secs. 21014(f)-(g), 21033].
Why? The proponents frame CEQA delay and litigation as a driver of California’s high housing, energy, and infrastructure costs. Their stated purpose is to “make California more affordable by streamlining and speeding up approval of essential projects” while keeping the state’s other environmental laws intact [1, Secs. 21011-21012].
4. Trade-offs
CEQA review and the lawsuits that follow can add years and cost to housing and infrastructure, and the delay is not evenly aimed at the most polluting projects. The legislature itself has spent recent sessions passing narrower CEQA exemptions for infill housing and other priorities, which shows that the cost-of-building concern is bipartisan and real, not manufactured. Proposition 45 is the broadest response yet because it does by initiative, and across seven whole project categories, what the legislature has done piecemeal.
Every lever the measure pulls to go faster also removes a check that CEQA built in on purpose. Hard deadlines with a “deemed complete” default speed things up, and they also let a clock, rather than a finished analysis, decide when review ends. A one-alternative EIR is cheaper and quicker, and it also means the public document may never study the option that would have reduced harm the most. The substantial-evidence standard and the bar on rescinding approvals cut litigation risk for builders, and they also make it harder for a neighbor or a tribe to stop a project that was genuinely under-analyzed. None of these is a free lunch. Each is a real gain in speed bought with a real reduction in review.
Two things keep this from being a simple pro-building versus pro-environment fight. First, the measure leaves the substantive environmental statutes standing. A project that violates the Clean Water Act or the Endangered Species Act is still illegal under those laws. What changes is CEQA’s procedural review, which is disclosure and analysis, not the pollution limits themselves. Second, the fight will be about the word “essential.” The definitions are broad. “Essential clean energy” reaches carbon-capture and hydrogen infrastructure, and the categories sweep in “related and ancillary” infrastructure as part of the “whole of the project.” How wide that lane runs, and how much of California’s building actually qualifies, is the question the ballot label cannot answer [1, Secs. 21028(f), (h)].
Many CEQA issues are not about acceptable levels of environmental damage. Instead, project opponents use procedural complaints under CEQA to slow down projects that they dislike for reasons having nothing to do with the environment. The proposition’s backers wish to reduce the use of CEQA for such purposes.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It replaces open-ended CEQA timelines with firm deadlines, which can cut the years of delay that raise the cost of housing, water, clean energy, and hospitals [1, Secs. 21018-21019].
The streamlined one-alternative EIR reduces the cost and length of environmental review while still requiring a “no project” comparison [1, Sec. 21025].
Tighter judicial rules, a 270-day case clock, and a bar on rescinding approvals reduce the litigation risk that can stall financing on approved projects [1, Secs. 21026-21027].
The LAO expects state and local governments to see long-run net savings from reduced administrative and legal workload once the system is running.
It leaves the underlying pollution-control statutes—the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act, and Coastal Act—in force, so it narrows CEQA procedure rather than repealing environmental protection [1, Sec. 21011(h)].
Potential risks
A one-alternative EIR and a “deemed complete” default can end review before the analysis is finished, so real environmental or community harms may go unstudied [1, Secs. 21017, 21025].
The bar on rescinding an approval and on challenging later construction approvals sharply limits the public’s ability to stop an under-reviewed project [1, Sec. 21027(d)-(e)].
The “essential project” definitions are broad and include ancillary infrastructure, so fights over what qualifies will be frequent and consequential [1, Sec. 21028(h)].
The LAO estimates implementation costs in the tens of millions of dollars annually for the first several years, with uncertain long-run court effects that could run from savings to added costs.
The self-defense clause commits an open-ended general fund appropriation to hired outside counsel if state officials decline to defend the measure [1, Section 4].
6. Open questions
How much of California’s actual building pipeline meets the “essential project” definition once ancillary infrastructure and the seven categories are counted?
Will the 365 business-day and 90 business-day clocks, which run longer than calendar deadlines, deliver the speed proponents promise?
Does limiting an EIR to one applicant-designed alternative meaningfully weaken the document’s ability to surface lower-impact options?
How will courts read “objective, quantifiable, and written standards” as the new test for a valid CEQA challenge, and how many suits does that screen out?
If the measure passes, how much litigation will target the boundaries of the definitions themselves, and who pays for the state’s defense under the independent-counsel clause?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
CEQA delay is a real driver of what it costs to build housing, water projects, and energy capacity in California. Proposition 45 speeds up those projects by shortening deadlines, shrinking the alternatives study, and limiting lawsuits. The questions are whether faster building is worth a lighter environmental and public review and whether to trust the broad definition of “essential” to stay in its lane.
Every provision that makes a project go faster also removes a check that CEQA put there on purpose. Which risk weighs more: a needed project stalled for years by process and litigation or a harmful project approved before the harm was fully studied?

Opinion: Prop. 45 will take a meat axe to California environmental
protections
Date: October 26, 2026
Source: East Bay Times: Web Edition Articles (CA)
Section: Commentary
Author: Deborah A Sivas
Word Count: 692
However well-intentioned, support for Proposition 45 is deeply misguided. It is true that California, like most states, needs
to build more housing, renewable energy projects, and other 21st century infrastructure. But eviscerating the California
Environmental Quality Act won't do that.
At its core, CEQA is a "stop, look, and listen" law. It requires government officials to make informed decisions by
considering the environmental impacts of projects, evaluating less impactful alternatives and other ways to mitigate
adverse effects, and soliciting public input from affected communities. CEQA itself cannot prevent projects from going
forward, but it can make developers and agencies think harder about designing them in the most sustainable way.
Since CEQA's passage more than 50 years ago, developers have been trying to kill it. Their efforts have recently gained
momentum as the "Abundance" narrative has taken hold. The general concept, as the best-seller of the same name tells
us, is to rid public decisions of "paperwork and procedure and hearings and disclosure demands and lawsuits" — the very
public process innovations that have made government more accountable to constituents and significantly reduced air
and water pollution.
The California Legislature has already responded to industry concerns over project delays, repeatedly tinkering with
CEQA's provisions to help expedite the review process. The most significant of these amendments came in June 2025,
with passage of AB 130 and SB 131. These new laws exempt most urban housing from CEQA altogether and streamline
the review process for many other projects.
Developers are not content to let these substantial CEQA reforms play out. Instead, they have taken advantage of the
"Abundance" movement with an industry-funded voter initiative that goes far beyond streamlining. Proposition 45 would,
among other things, give developers new litigation rights to sue local agencies over even shorter approval deadlines,
allow developers to replace the normal "reasonable range of alternatives" that officials must consider with a single,
developer-designed onsite "alternative," and reduce the ability of the public to comment on projects.
Most troubling, Proposition 45 so severely constrains judicial review as to make CEQA meaningless. Courts finding an
environmental analysis legally deficient could not prevent the project from going forward while the CEQA flaws are
remedied. That is, the developer could build the project before the impacts are properly evaluated. This single provision
renders CEQA nothing more than a paper tiger.
And here's the kicker: If passed, Proposition 45 would prohibit future statutory amendments unless they (1) affirmatively
"further" the newly-declared statutory purpose of "streamlining and speeding approval of essential projects" and (2) are
enacted by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature. In short, developers want to disenfranchise communities in perpetuity.
The non-profit Rose Foundation has published several empirical studies (in 2016, 2021, and 2023) confirming that CEQA
affects only a very small fraction of housing projects. These studies refute the methodology and conclusions advanced in
a 2017 report by the industry's favorite private law firm.
The reasons for project delays are myriad — misaligned financial incentives, skilled labor shortages, outdated building
codes, vocal public opposition, and yes, occasionally CEQA lawsuits. The Legislature has steadily addressed these
obstacles in targeted reforms, especially with respect to housing. Instead of a surgical scalpel, Prop 45 takes a meat axe
to the law. That is likely why even the very pro-housing YIMBY movement takes no position on the initiative and why most
environmental groups and many local officials strongly oppose it.
CEQA promotes decision transparency, agency accountability, and public participation. It has significantly reduced
pollution and unsustainable resource exploitation. And it is virtually the only tool available to communities facing public
health and environmental impacts from sprawling projects like data centers, Amazon warehouses, and expanding oil
fields. Proposition 45 attempts to deprive Californians of a meaningful say in their own future, while doing nothing to make
housing more affordable or available.
Deborah A. Sivas is a professor of environmental law at Stanford Law and of environmental social science at the Doerr
School of Sustainability.

Proposition 45 would carve a new fast-track lane through the California Environmental Quality Act for what it calls “essential projects.” It adds a new chapter, Chapter 1.5, to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code, the part of state law that is CEQA. PROP 45: The CEQA “Essential Projects” Fast Track (Building an Affordable California Act)
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%2045.pdf)
Research
