California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney General title and summary, December 26, 2025)
Measure’s own name: The Building an Affordable California Act (AG No. 25-0023A1)
Type: Initiated state statute
A vote YES means: A new “essential projects” category (most housing, water, clean energy, medical, public safety, broadband, and transportation projects) gets hard deadlines for CEQA review, a slimmed-down alternatives analysis, and tighter limits on lawsuits, all written into the Public Resources Code [1, Sec. 21013].
A vote NO means: CEQA’s existing review timelines, alternatives requirements, and judicial-review rules stay in place for these projects.
Sponsor/proponent: California Chamber of Commerce. Proponent of record: Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer LLP.
On the ballot because: Qualified by random-sample signature check on June 16, 2026, and certified eligible June 25, 2026. The measure needed 546,651 valid signatures.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0023 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-023)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 45 would carve a new fast-track lane through the California Environmental Quality Act for what it calls “essential projects.” It adds a new chapter, Chapter 1.5, to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code, the part of state law that is CEQA. It does not repeal CEQA, and it does not touch the other environmental statutes it names, such as the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the California Coastal Act. What it changes is CEQA’s procedure for a defined set of projects [1, Sec. 1 (21011(h)), 21012-21033].
The measure does three main things for essential projects. First, it puts public agencies on a clock. An agency has thirty days to decide whether an application is complete or the application is deemed complete automatically. Once complete, a lead agency has 365 days to decide whether to certify an environmental impact report (EIR), 180 days to act on a negative declaration, and 90 days to document an exemption. For the 365-day and 90-day review clocks the measure counts only business days, not weekends or state holidays, so the real-world calendar is longer than the raw numbers suggest [1, Secs. 21017-21019, 21028(c)].
Second, it shrinks the alternatives analysis. Today a CEQA environmental impact report must study a reasonable range of alternatives to a project. Under Proposition 45, an EIR for an essential project needs to analyze only the project itself, one alternative developed by the applicant, and the “no project” alternative. The measure declares that any additional alternatives are “unnecessary” and that no agency may require them [1, Sec. 21025].
Third, it narrows the courtroom. A challenger must sue within thirty days of the agency’s notice of determination, the case must finish within 270 days including any appeal, and the court must use the deferential substantial-evidence standard rather than independent judgment. A court that finds a defect may order the agency to redo only the specific study at issue. It “may not order or direct” the agency to rescind its approval of the project, and once a project clears review its later construction and implementation approvals cannot be challenged again [1, Secs. 21026-21027].
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (amended language submitted November 24, 2025)
Key language:
“‘Essential project’ means a project that meets all of the following requirements … The project does not include a jail or other detention facility, or involve the development of a new oil or natural gas production facility.” [1, Sec. 21028(h)]
“A court may not order or direct via writ or any other form of order, injunction, or decision that an agency rescind its approval of the essential project.” [1, Sec. 21027(d)]
What it amends: Adds Chapter 1.5 (commencing with Section 21010) to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code. Because it is an initiative statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, but only in ways that further the measure’s purposes unless it says otherwise. The measure also adds a self-defense clause. If the governor and attorney general both decline to defend it in court, the attorney general must appoint independent counsel, funded by a continuous general fund appropriation [1, Secs. 21010, Section 4].
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, with the initiative filed by attorney Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer. Supporters include the California Building Industry Association, the California Hospital Association, NAACP California, and Pacific Gas and Electric. Opposition is led by environmental organizations, including Sierra Club California, the Planning and Conservation League, and CalBike.
What? A new “essential projects” category covering most housing, water, clean energy, medical, public-safety, broadband, and transportation projects, given fixed review deadlines, a one-alternative EIR, and tighter judicial review. Jails and detention facilities and new oil and gas production facilities are excluded, and by definition Delta conveyance and high-speed rail are left out of the water and transportation categories. [1, Secs. 21013, 21028].
Where? Statewide, applied to all public agencies and written into the Public Resources Code [1, Sec. 21014(d)].
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. It takes effect the day after the election if it passes and applies to applications deemed complete after that date, including projects that withdraw and resubmit to opt in [1, Secs. 21014(f)-(g), 21033].
Why? The proponents frame CEQA delay and litigation as a driver of California’s high housing, energy, and infrastructure costs. Their stated purpose is to “make California more affordable by streamlining and speeding up approval of essential projects” while keeping the state’s other environmental laws intact [1, Secs. 21011-21012].
4. Trade-offs
CEQA review and the lawsuits that follow can add years and cost to housing and infrastructure, and the delay is not evenly aimed at the most polluting projects. The legislature itself has spent recent sessions passing narrower CEQA exemptions for infill housing and other priorities, which shows that the cost-of-building concern is bipartisan and real, not manufactured. Proposition 45 is the broadest response yet because it does by initiative, and across seven whole project categories, what the legislature has done piecemeal.
Every lever the measure pulls to go faster also removes a check that CEQA built in on purpose. Hard deadlines with a “deemed complete” default speed things up, and they also let a clock, rather than a finished analysis, decide when review ends. A one-alternative EIR is cheaper and quicker, and it also means the public document may never study the option that would have reduced harm the most. The substantial-evidence standard and the bar on rescinding approvals cut litigation risk for builders, and they also make it harder for a neighbor or a tribe to stop a project that was genuinely under-analyzed. None of these is a free lunch. Each is a real gain in speed bought with a real reduction in review.
Two things keep this from being a simple pro-building versus pro-environment fight. First, the measure leaves the substantive environmental statutes standing. A project that violates the Clean Water Act or the Endangered Species Act is still illegal under those laws. What changes is CEQA’s procedural review, which is disclosure and analysis, not the pollution limits themselves. Second, the fight will be about the word “essential.” The definitions are broad. “Essential clean energy” reaches carbon-capture and hydrogen infrastructure, and the categories sweep in “related and ancillary” infrastructure as part of the “whole of the project.” How wide that lane runs, and how much of California’s building actually qualifies, is the question the ballot label cannot answer [1, Secs. 21028(f), (h)].
Many CEQA issues are not about acceptable levels of environmental damage. Instead, project opponents use procedural complaints under CEQA to slow down projects that they dislike for reasons having nothing to do with the environment. The proposition’s backers wish to reduce the use of CEQA for such purposes.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It replaces open-ended CEQA timelines with firm deadlines, which can cut the years of delay that raise the cost of housing, water, clean energy, and hospitals [1, Secs. 21018-21019].
The streamlined one-alternative EIR reduces the cost and length of environmental review while still requiring a “no project” comparison [1, Sec. 21025].
Tighter judicial rules, a 270-day case clock, and a bar on rescinding approvals reduce the litigation risk that can stall financing on approved projects [1, Secs. 21026-21027].
The LAO expects state and local governments to see long-run net savings from reduced administrative and legal workload once the system is running.
It leaves the underlying pollution-control statutes—the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act, and Coastal Act—in force, so it narrows CEQA procedure rather than repealing environmental protection [1, Sec. 21011(h)].
Potential risks
A one-alternative EIR and a “deemed complete” default can end review before the analysis is finished, so real environmental or community harms may go unstudied [1, Secs. 21017, 21025].
The bar on rescinding an approval and on challenging later construction approvals sharply limits the public’s ability to stop an under-reviewed project [1, Sec. 21027(d)-(e)].
The “essential project” definitions are broad and include ancillary infrastructure, so fights over what qualifies will be frequent and consequential [1, Sec. 21028(h)].
The LAO estimates implementation costs in the tens of millions of dollars annually for the first several years, with uncertain long-run court effects that could run from savings to added costs.
The self-defense clause commits an open-ended general fund appropriation to hired outside counsel if state officials decline to defend the measure [1, Section 4].
6. Open questions
How much of California’s actual building pipeline meets the “essential project” definition once ancillary infrastructure and the seven categories are counted?
Will the 365 business-day and 90 business-day clocks, which run longer than calendar deadlines, deliver the speed proponents promise?
Does limiting an EIR to one applicant-designed alternative meaningfully weaken the document’s ability to surface lower-impact options?
How will courts read “objective, quantifiable, and written standards” as the new test for a valid CEQA challenge, and how many suits does that screen out?
If the measure passes, how much litigation will target the boundaries of the definitions themselves, and who pays for the state’s defense under the independent-counsel clause?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
CEQA delay is a real driver of what it costs to build housing, water projects, and energy capacity in California. Proposition 45 speeds up those projects by shortening deadlines, shrinking the alternatives study, and limiting lawsuits. The questions are whether faster building is worth a lighter environmental and public review and whether to trust the broad definition of “essential” to stay in its lane.
Every provision that makes a project go faster also removes a check that CEQA put there on purpose. Which risk weighs more: a needed project stalled for years by process and litigation or a harmful project approved before the harm was fully studied?

Opinion: Prop. 45 will take a meat axe to California environmental
protections
Date: October 26, 2026
Source: East Bay Times: Web Edition Articles (CA)
Section: Commentary
Author: Deborah A Sivas
Word Count: 692
However well-intentioned, support for Proposition 45 is deeply misguided. It is true that California, like most states, needs
to build more housing, renewable energy projects, and other 21st century infrastructure. But eviscerating the California
Environmental Quality Act won't do that.
At its core, CEQA is a "stop, look, and listen" law. It requires government officials to make informed decisions by
considering the environmental impacts of projects, evaluating less impactful alternatives and other ways to mitigate
adverse effects, and soliciting public input from affected communities. CEQA itself cannot prevent projects from going
forward, but it can make developers and agencies think harder about designing them in the most sustainable way.
Since CEQA's passage more than 50 years ago, developers have been trying to kill it. Their efforts have recently gained
momentum as the "Abundance" narrative has taken hold. The general concept, as the best-seller of the same name tells
us, is to rid public decisions of "paperwork and procedure and hearings and disclosure demands and lawsuits" — the very
public process innovations that have made government more accountable to constituents and significantly reduced air
and water pollution.
The California Legislature has already responded to industry concerns over project delays, repeatedly tinkering with
CEQA's provisions to help expedite the review process. The most significant of these amendments came in June 2025,
with passage of AB 130 and SB 131. These new laws exempt most urban housing from CEQA altogether and streamline
the review process for many other projects.
Developers are not content to let these substantial CEQA reforms play out. Instead, they have taken advantage of the
"Abundance" movement with an industry-funded voter initiative that goes far beyond streamlining. Proposition 45 would,
among other things, give developers new litigation rights to sue local agencies over even shorter approval deadlines,
allow developers to replace the normal "reasonable range of alternatives" that officials must consider with a single,
developer-designed onsite "alternative," and reduce the ability of the public to comment on projects.
Most troubling, Proposition 45 so severely constrains judicial review as to make CEQA meaningless. Courts finding an
environmental analysis legally deficient could not prevent the project from going forward while the CEQA flaws are
remedied. That is, the developer could build the project before the impacts are properly evaluated. This single provision
renders CEQA nothing more than a paper tiger.
And here's the kicker: If passed, Proposition 45 would prohibit future statutory amendments unless they (1) affirmatively
"further" the newly-declared statutory purpose of "streamlining and speeding approval of essential projects" and (2) are
enacted by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature. In short, developers want to disenfranchise communities in perpetuity.
The non-profit Rose Foundation has published several empirical studies (in 2016, 2021, and 2023) confirming that CEQA
affects only a very small fraction of housing projects. These studies refute the methodology and conclusions advanced in
a 2017 report by the industry's favorite private law firm.
The reasons for project delays are myriad — misaligned financial incentives, skilled labor shortages, outdated building
codes, vocal public opposition, and yes, occasionally CEQA lawsuits. The Legislature has steadily addressed these
obstacles in targeted reforms, especially with respect to housing. Instead of a surgical scalpel, Prop 45 takes a meat axe
to the law. That is likely why even the very pro-housing YIMBY movement takes no position on the initiative and why most
environmental groups and many local officials strongly oppose it.
CEQA promotes decision transparency, agency accountability, and public participation. It has significantly reduced
pollution and unsustainable resource exploitation. And it is virtually the only tool available to communities facing public
health and environmental impacts from sprawling projects like data centers, Amazon warehouses, and expanding oil
fields. Proposition 45 attempts to deprive Californians of a meaningful say in their own future, while doing nothing to make
housing more affordable or available.
Deborah A. Sivas is a professor of environmental law at Stanford Law and of environmental social science at the Doerr
School of Sustainability.

A court that finds a defect may order the agency to redo only the specific study at issue. It “may not order or direct” the agency to rescind its approval of the project, and once a project clears review its later construction and implementation approvals cannot be challenged again [1, Secs. 21026-21027].
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (amended language submitted November 24, 2025)
Key language:
“‘Essential project’ means a project that meets all of the following requirements … The project does not include a jail or other detention facility, or involve the development of a new oil or natural gas production facility.” [1, Sec. 21028(h)]
“A court may not order or direct via writ or any other form of order, injunction, or decision that an agency rescind its approval of the essential project.” [1, Sec. 21027(d)]
What it amends: Adds Chapter 1.5 (commencing with Section 21010) to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code. Because it is an initiative statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, but only in ways that further the measure’s purposes unless it says otherwise. The measure also adds a self-defense clause. If the governor and attorney general both decline to defend it in court, the attorney general must appoint independent counsel, funded by a continuous general fund appropriation [1, Secs. 21010, Section 4].
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, with the initiative filed by attorney Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer. Supporters include the California Building Industry Association, the California Hospital Association, NAACP California, and Pacific Gas and Electric. Opposition is led by environmental organizations, including Sierra Club California, the Planning and Conservation League, and CalBike.
What? A new “essential projects” category covering most housing, water, clean energy, medical, public-safety, broadband, and transportation projects, given fixed review deadlines, a one-alternative EIR, and tighter judicial review. Jails and detention facilities and new oil and gas production facilities are excluded, and by definition Delta conveyance and high-speed rail are left out of the water and transportation categories. [1, Secs. 21013, 21028].
Where? Statewide, applied to all public agencies and written into the Public Resources Code [1, Sec. 21014(d)].
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. It takes effect the day after the election if it passes and applies to applications deemed complete after that date, including projects that withdraw and resubmit to opt in [1, Secs. 21014(f)-(g), 21033].
Why? The proponents frame CEQA delay and litigation as a driver of California’s high housing, energy, and infrastructure costs. Their stated purpose is to “make California more affordable by streamlining and speeding up approval of essential projects” while keeping the state’s other environmental laws intact [1, Secs. 21011-21012].
4. Trade-offs
CEQA review and the lawsuits that follow can add years and cost to housing and infrastructure, and the delay is not evenly aimed at the most polluting projects. The legislature itself has spent recent sessions passing narrower CEQA exemptions for infill housing and other priorities, which shows that the cost-of-building concern is bipartisan and real, not manufactured. Proposition 45 is the broadest response yet because it does by initiative, and across seven whole project categories, what the legislature has done piecemeal.
Every lever the measure pulls to go faster also removes a check that CEQA built in on purpose. Hard deadlines with a “deemed complete” default speed things up, and they also let a clock, rather than a finished analysis, decide when review ends. A one-alternative EIR is cheaper and quicker, and it also means the public document may never study the option that would have reduced harm the most. The substantial-evidence standard and the bar on rescinding approvals cut litigation risk for builders, and they also make it harder for a neighbor or a tribe to stop a project that was genuinely under-analyzed. None of these is a free lunch. Each is a real gain in speed bought with a real reduction in review.
Two things keep this from being a simple pro-building versus pro-environment fight. First, the measure leaves the substantive environmental statutes standing. A project that violates the Clean Water Act or the Endangered Species Act is still illegal under those laws. What changes is CEQA’s procedural review, which is disclosure and analysis, not the pollution limits themselves. Second, the fight will be about the word “essential.” The definitions are broad. “Essential clean energy” reaches carbon-capture and hydrogen infrastructure, and the categories sweep in “related and ancillary” infrastructure as part of the “whole of the project.” How wide that lane runs, and how much of California’s building actually qualifies, is the question the ballot label cannot answer [1, Secs. 21028(f), (h)].
Many CEQA issues are not about acceptable levels of environmental damage. Instead, project opponents use procedural complaints under CEQA to slow down projects that they dislike for reasons having nothing to do with the environment. The proposition’s backers wish to reduce the use of CEQA for such purposes.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It replaces open-ended CEQA timelines with firm deadlines, which can cut the years of delay that raise the cost of housing, water, clean energy, and hospitals [1, Secs. 21018-21019].
The streamlined one-alternative EIR reduces the cost and length of environmental review while still requiring a “no project” comparison [1, Sec. 21025].
Tighter judicial rules, a 270-day case clock, and a bar on rescinding approvals reduce the litigation risk that can stall financing on approved projects [1, Secs. 21026-21027].
The LAO expects state and local governments to see long-run net savings from reduced administrative and legal workload once the system is running.
It leaves the underlying pollution-control statutes—the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act, and Coastal Act—in force, so it narrows CEQA procedure rather than repealing environmental protection [1, Sec. 21011(h)].
Potential risks
A one-alternative EIR and a “deemed complete” default can end review before the analysis is finished, so real environmental or community harms may go unstudied [1, Secs. 21017, 21025].
The bar on rescinding an approval and on challenging later construction approvals sharply limits the public’s ability to stop an under-reviewed project [1, Sec. 21027(d)-(e)].
The “essential project” definitions are broad and include ancillary infrastructure, so fights over what qualifies will be frequent and consequential [1, Sec. 21028(h)].
The LAO estimates implementation costs in the tens of millions of dollars annually for the first several years, with uncertain long-run court effects that could run from savings to added costs.
The self-defense clause commits an open-ended general fund appropriation to hired outside counsel if state officials decline to defend the measure [1, Section 4].
6. Open questions
How much of California’s actual building pipeline meets the “essential project” definition once ancillary infrastructure and the seven categories are counted?
Will the 365 business-day and 90 business-day clocks, which run longer than calendar deadlines, deliver the speed proponents promise?
Does limiting an EIR to one applicant-designed alternative meaningfully weaken the document’s ability to surface lower-impact options?
How will courts read “objective, quantifiable, and written standards” as the new test for a valid CEQA challenge, and how many suits does that screen out?
If the measure passes, how much litigation will target the boundaries of the definitions themselves, and who pays for the state’s defense under the independent-counsel clause?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
CEQA delay is a real driver of what it costs to build housing, water projects, and energy capacity in California. Proposition 45 speeds up those projects by shortening deadlines, shrinking the alternatives study, and limiting lawsuits. The questions are whether faster building is worth a lighter environmental and public review and whether to trust the broad definition of “essential” to stay in its lane.
Every provision that makes a project go faster also removes a check that CEQA put there on purpose. Which risk weighs more: a needed project stalled for years by process and litigation or a harmful project approved before the harm was fully studied?

Opinion: Prop. 45 will take a meat axe to California environmental
protections
Date: October 26, 2026
Source: East Bay Times: Web Edition Articles (CA)
Section: Commentary
Author: Deborah A Sivas
Word Count: 692
However well-intentioned, support for Proposition 45 is deeply misguided. It is true that California, like most states, needs
to build more housing, renewable energy projects, and other 21st century infrastructure. But eviscerating the California
Environmental Quality Act won't do that.
At its core, CEQA is a "stop, look, and listen" law. It requires government officials to make informed decisions by
considering the environmental impacts of projects, evaluating less impactful alternatives and other ways to mitigate
adverse effects, and soliciting public input from affected communities. CEQA itself cannot prevent projects from going
forward, but it can make developers and agencies think harder about designing them in the most sustainable way.
Since CEQA's passage more than 50 years ago, developers have been trying to kill it. Their efforts have recently gained
momentum as the "Abundance" narrative has taken hold. The general concept, as the best-seller of the same name tells
us, is to rid public decisions of "paperwork and procedure and hearings and disclosure demands and lawsuits" — the very
public process innovations that have made government more accountable to constituents and significantly reduced air
and water pollution.
The California Legislature has already responded to industry concerns over project delays, repeatedly tinkering with
CEQA's provisions to help expedite the review process. The most significant of these amendments came in June 2025,
with passage of AB 130 and SB 131. These new laws exempt most urban housing from CEQA altogether and streamline
the review process for many other projects.
Developers are not content to let these substantial CEQA reforms play out. Instead, they have taken advantage of the
"Abundance" movement with an industry-funded voter initiative that goes far beyond streamlining. Proposition 45 would,
among other things, give developers new litigation rights to sue local agencies over even shorter approval deadlines,
allow developers to replace the normal "reasonable range of alternatives" that officials must consider with a single,
developer-designed onsite "alternative," and reduce the ability of the public to comment on projects.
Most troubling, Proposition 45 so severely constrains judicial review as to make CEQA meaningless. Courts finding an
environmental analysis legally deficient could not prevent the project from going forward while the CEQA flaws are
remedied. That is, the developer could build the project before the impacts are properly evaluated. This single provision
renders CEQA nothing more than a paper tiger.
And here's the kicker: If passed, Proposition 45 would prohibit future statutory amendments unless they (1) affirmatively
"further" the newly-declared statutory purpose of "streamlining and speeding approval of essential projects" and (2) are
enacted by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature. In short, developers want to disenfranchise communities in perpetuity.
The non-profit Rose Foundation has published several empirical studies (in 2016, 2021, and 2023) confirming that CEQA
affects only a very small fraction of housing projects. These studies refute the methodology and conclusions advanced in
a 2017 report by the industry's favorite private law firm.
The reasons for project delays are myriad — misaligned financial incentives, skilled labor shortages, outdated building
codes, vocal public opposition, and yes, occasionally CEQA lawsuits. The Legislature has steadily addressed these
obstacles in targeted reforms, especially with respect to housing. Instead of a surgical scalpel, Prop 45 takes a meat axe
to the law. That is likely why even the very pro-housing YIMBY movement takes no position on the initiative and why most
environmental groups and many local officials strongly oppose it.
CEQA promotes decision transparency, agency accountability, and public participation. It has significantly reduced
pollution and unsustainable resource exploitation. And it is virtually the only tool available to communities facing public
health and environmental impacts from sprawling projects like data centers, Amazon warehouses, and expanding oil
fields. Proposition 45 attempts to deprive Californians of a meaningful say in their own future, while doing nothing to make
housing more affordable or available.
Deborah A. Sivas is a professor of environmental law at Stanford Law and of environmental social science at the Doerr
School of Sustainability.

- The measure's most troubling features (per neutral/near-neutral legal experts): (a) locks in "existing laws" as of application date, freezing environmental standards; (b) narrows judicial review to "objective existing laws" — arguably rendering CEQA's core "significant effect" analysis unenforceable; (c) courts cannot stop a project even if review was deficient (only the noncomplying part), and injunctions require "clear and convincing evidence" of a "specific, adverse impact upon public safety"; (d) one applicant-designed alternative, presumed to lessen impacts; (e) capped comment periods and exclusion of late comments from the record, plus no new comment period if the project changes in response to comments; (f) two-thirds legislative vote to amend + must "further" the chapter's purposes = effectively permanent; (g) excludes non-federally-recognized tribes from consultation (dozens of tribes, including in Bay Area, Central Coast, LA); (h) occupies the field + controls over conflicting law + frozen statutory cross-references as of Dec 31, 2025; (i) continuous general fund appropriation for independent counsel to defend it; (j) broad "essential" definitions incl. ancillary infrastructure, ambiguity re data centers/warehouses, wildfire "vegetation management" (could cover commercial logging); (k) developer right to sue agencies over denials/conditions; (l) "fullest possible weight" to approval — a pro-approval interpretive thumb on the scale.
- LAO: initial costs high tens of millions to >$100M annually; longer-term uncertain.
- Notably, the coalition is unusual: California Democratic Party, California Labor Federation, State Building & Construction Trades Council, League of Women Voters, Sierra Club, NRDC, Center for Biological Diversity, Earthjustice oppose; while business/developers/utilities/homebuilders, CA Republican Party, hospitals, water association, some affordable housing groups, LULAC, NAACP CA support. Editorial boards split: 28 newspapers Yes (incl. SD Union-Tribune, SCNG's 11 papers, McClatchy CA board incl. Sacramento Bee, Mercury News/East Bay Times); SF Chronicle No; LA Times columnist Skelton No.
- Many prominent CEQA reformers (Wiener, CA YIMBY, YIMBY Action, SPUR, Abundant Housing LA, Tom Steyer) neutral or opposed — an important signal: the people most committed to fixing CEQA don't think this is the right fix. That's a strong indicator that this measure is overbroad/poorly drafted.
- Polling: PPIC Oct 2026: 46% yes / 50% no — likely to fail or be very close.

Given the "irreversibility" (two-thirds amendment requirement, must further purposes), the interpretive thumb toward approval, the narrowing of judicial review to "objective existing laws" (which likely guts CEQA's substantive check), the freezing of standards at application date, the exclusion of non-federally recognized tribes, the continuous appropriation for private counsel, the broad and ambiguous "essential" definitions, and the fact that the Legislature has already passed targeted reforms (AB 130/SB 131) and can continue doing so — while Prop 45 would lock in a badly drafted, one-sided overhaul that can't be fixed without a two-thirds vote — I lean NO.

Counter-consideration: The genuine problem of CEQA abuse/delay is real, and the measure has some reasonable features (deadlines, one-shot completeness corrections list, 270-day judicial clock). Also there's an argument that voting No preserves a status quo that delays clean energy and housing. But the measure is an initiative statute that cannot be amended except by 2/3 vote in a direction that furthers streamlining — a huge red flag for a 41-page, complex, ambiguous law that even its supporters admit will generate litigation over its scope (data centers). And critically, the Legislature remains free to pass targeted CEQA reform after a No vote (as it has repeatedly done); a No doesn't freeze anything. Whereas a Yes locks in a pro-approval thumb and near-permanent constraints.

Also worth weighing: the fiscal cost (LAO), the removal of the court's power to halt a project pending correction of a deficient EIR — which Sivas calls rendering CEQA "a paper tiger." And the "vested rights"/existing-laws freeze which could undermine the state's ability to update environmental protections.

I'm fairly confident in NO. Support for billionaire tax, permitting reform measures both drop in new polling
By Andrew Graham
October 27, 2026 9:00 PM
Susan Silva fills out her ballot at the vote center at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. A new poll from the Public Policy Institute of California found just 46% of likely voters will support the billionaire’s tax.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Support for a ballot measure to tax billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317272374.html) slid six points since September as California’s ultra-wealthy class spend hundreds of millions of dollars opposing (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317386167.html) the measure, according to a newly released poll from the Public Policy Institute of California released one week before the Nov. 3 election.
The October poll found just 46% (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 40, the billionaire’s tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317075667.html), while 52% would vote no. That’s a flip from the September polling, when 52% of likely voters considered themselves a Yes vote. The latest polling was conducted from Oct. 16 to Oct. 22.
The 6% lead for the No side falls outside the poll’s margin of error, which was around 3% according to PPIC.
The decline was among the most noteworthy changes in polling about the November ballot, PPIC poll director Mark Baldassare told The Sacramento Bee. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra maintained a 24-point lead over Republican Steve Hilton (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317800503.html) in the governor’s race, up from a 22-point lead in September. A majority of voters continue to tell pollsters they’re more likely to vote for a Democrat than a Republican for the U.S. House, though the survey does not break down the state’s contested battleground district races (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317708380.html).
» Election news in your inbox: Sign up for our election newsletter here (https://www.sacbee.com/newsletters?newsletter=sacramento_election_newsletter&storylink=inline_story_link_cf)
Proposition 45 slips into minority support
Meanwhile, the split over another of the election cycle’s most contentious measures, a bid to reform permitting under (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317756293.html) the California Environmental Quality Act, remained tight. However, for the first time in PPIC’s polling the measure, Proposition 45, faces opposition from a slim majority of likely voters. Now, 50% of respondents told PPIC’s pollsters they’d vote against it, while 46% said they planned to back it and 4% remain undecided.
A month ago, 49% of likely voters said they were a yes on the measure, while 46% were a no.
Prop. 45 would impose deadlines on agencies to complete CEQA reviews and on courts to resolve lawsuits for eight categories of building projects. Proponents, which include business interests, home builders and utility companies, say it will speed projects that California communities are dying to build, but that are hampered by cost increases and delays from CEQA litigation. Opponents say it too heavily tilts the judicial and regulatory scales toward approving projects over community objections. It also gives developers a route to sue the government over project denials.
The tight margins, after campaigning by both sides, show the measure is a tricky one (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705781.html) for Californians who value environmental protections but are frustrated by the state’s high housing and utility costs, Baldassare said. In the same survey data, more than half of Californians named the cost of living, inflation and housing costs as the most important issues facing the state.
“This is a tough one for people to figure out how they should vote on this,” Baldassare said of Prop. 45. “I think it’s one of the propositions that people are most conflicted about.”
The tight polling reflects divides around the proposal that have played out in some unusual ways. Though a majority of Republican voters favors Prop. 45, 41% remain opposed in the latest PPIC poll, and some county-level Republican parties have split (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317563736.html) from the state central committee, which endorsed it. Affordable housing groups have also split over the measure, and some prominent elected Democratic officials who have called for CEQA reforms in the past, such as Gov. Gavin Newsom, have stayed on the sidelines (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317625735.html).
The California Democratic Party opposes Prop. 45 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316736860.html), and the coalition against it is composed principally of environmental organizations and labor unions (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317611394.html).
The two sides have clashed mightily over data centers (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705781.html), which are broadly unpopular with the public and which the No campaign says could make a bid for the streamlined permitting process, something the Yes side strenuously denies.
Voters in earlier polling indicated broad support for reforming CEQA, if not necessarily for the specifics of Prop. 45. Of likely voters, 73% told PPIC this summer they’d vote yes on a proposal to modify environmental reviews for housing, transportation, health, water and clean energy projects. At the time the question did not carry the specific ballot language for the measure.
Election security
PPIC’s pollsters were calling voters amid an extraordinary period of clashes (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317690067.html) between federal and state officials over California’s election (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705634.html) security. U.S. Department of Justice attorneys sued the state in an attempt to force a review its voter rolls, and last week brought highly publicized charges against 28 California residents (https://www.sacbee.com/news/california/article317685125.html) they said voted illegally because they are not (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317689474.html) U.S. citizens. State officials have defended California’s electoral systems (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317738101.html) and accused the Trump administration of sowing doubt and chaos ahead of the midterm election.
A majority of Californians maintain confidence in the state’s ballot counting. Of likely voters, 63% have either “a great deal” or “quite a lot” of confidence in the state’s election system, according to the poll, while 15% said they had only “some confidence” and 22% said they had “very little confidence.” Seven in 10 likely voters support sending a vote-by-mail ballot to every active registered voter before each election.
Proposition 39, which is conservative Assemblymember Carl DeMaio’s answer to what he says are widespread, bipartisan concerns about the state’s election security, continued in the latest PPIC poll to be underwater, with just 41% saying they’d vote for it. Prop. 39 would require voters (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005401.html) to bring a government-issued ID to polling places or write the end of an identification number on mail ballots. It also requires county officials to scrub voter rolls for citizenship.
Loading…
As economic worries grow, Newsom’s popularity dips
Governor Newsom’s favorability ratings have dipped in the last months of his eight-year tenure as state leader. Just 47% of polled adults and 49% of likely voters told PPIC this month they approved of his job performance. It is the first time his job performance rating has dipped in the PPIC poll below 50% since last October. About 7 in 10 Democrats and 1 in 10 Republicans approve of the governor, and he is more popular in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles than elsewhere in California, PPIC found.
Newsom is widely considered to be planning a presidential bid in 2028. His dip in the polling this month seems less attributable to any new policy position or statements than to just a general gloom among California residents about the state’s direction, Baldassare said. A large majority of voters, 79% are pessimistic about the economy, around 73% say their income isn’t keeping up with inflation and 55% say the state is headed in the wrong direction.
“This is just general unhappiness,” Baldassare said. And, “what you’re seeing in our poll from that general unhappiness is now some majorities saying they disapprove of their governor and their Legislature.”

# New CEQA Study Says Housing and Infill Projects Dominate Appeals, Drawing Pushback from Prop. 45 Opponents
Vanguard News Group
West Coast Land Use and Environmental Group Leader Jennifer Hernandez was cited in a *Vanguard News Group* article recapping her most recent study on the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and her call to pass Proposition 45.
Holland & Knight's study analyzed CEQA appeals during an 11-year period and found residential projects accounted for a little more than 25 percent of cases, including infill developments within existing communities.
It also showed environmental impact reports, the most extensive form of CEQA review, factored in more than half of the appellate decisions, demonstrating how projects can become snarled in lawsuits and remained stalled for years.
Jennifer, who led the study, argues the data makes "an incontrovertible case for Proposition 45," which would create new environmental review, permitting and litigation procedures for projects such as housing, water and transportation, tighten deadlines for agencies to complete environmental reviews, and restrict the scope of evidence courts can consider when reviewing challenges to project approvals.
She argued these reforms would reduce litigation-driven delays while still preserving environmental protections.
"California should not have to choose between protecting the environment and building the housing and infrastructure we need," she said.

Support for billionaire tax, permitting reform measures both drop in new polling
By Andrew Graham
October 27, 2026 9:00 PM
Susan Silva fills out her ballot at the vote center at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. A new poll from the Public Policy Institute of California found just 46% of likely voters will support the billionaire’s tax.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Support for a ballot measure to tax billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317272374.html) slid six points since September as California’s ultra-wealthy class spend hundreds of millions of dollars opposing (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317386167.html) the measure, according to a newly released poll from the Public Policy Institute of California released one week before the Nov. 3 election.
The October poll found just 46% (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 40, the billionaire’s tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317075667.html), while 52% would vote no. That’s a flip from the September polling, when 52% of likely voters considered themselves a Yes vote. The latest polling was conducted from Oct. 16 to Oct. 22.
The 6% lead for the No side falls outside the poll’s margin of error, which was around 3% according to PPIC.
The decline was among the most noteworthy changes in polling about the November ballot, PPIC poll director Mark Baldassare told The Sacramento Bee. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra maintained a 24-point lead over Republican Steve Hilton (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317800503.html) in the governor’s race, up from a 22-point lead in September. A majority of voters continue to tell pollsters they’re more likely to vote for a Democrat than a Republican for the U.S. House, though the survey does not break down the state’s contested battleground district races (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317708380.html).

Proposition 45 slips into minority support
Meanwhile, the split over another of the election cycle’s most contentious measures, a bid to reform permitting under (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317756293.html) the California Environmental Quality Act, remained tight. However, for the first time in PPIC’s polling the measure, Proposition 45, faces opposition from a slim majority of likely voters. Now, 50% of respondents told PPIC’s pollsters they’d vote against it, while 46% said they planned to back it and 4% remain undecided.
A month ago, 49% of likely voters said they were a yes on the measure, while 46% were a no.
Prop. 45 would impose deadlines on agencies to complete CEQA reviews and on courts to resolve lawsuits for eight categories of building projects. Proponents, which include business interests, home builders and utility companies, say it will speed projects that California communities are dying to build, but that are hampered by cost increases and delays from CEQA litigation. Opponents say it too heavily tilts the judicial and regulatory scales toward approving projects over community objections. It also gives developers a route to sue the government over project denials.
The tight margins, after campaigning by both sides, show the measure is a tricky one (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705781.html) for Californians who value environmental protections but are frustrated by the state’s high housing and utility costs, Baldassare said. In the same survey data, more than half of Californians named the cost of living, inflation and housing costs as the most important issues facing the state.
“This is a tough one for people to figure out how they should vote on this,” Baldassare said of Prop. 45. “I think it’s one of the propositions that people are most conflicted about.”
The tight polling reflects divides around the proposal that have played out in some unusual ways. Though a majority of Republican voters favors Prop. 45, 41% remain opposed in the latest PPIC poll, and some county-level Republican parties have split (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317563736.html) from the state central committee, which endorsed it. Affordable housing groups have also split over the measure, and some prominent elected Democratic officials who have called for CEQA reforms in the past, such as Gov. Gavin Newsom, have stayed on the sidelines (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317625735.html).
The California Democratic Party opposes Prop. 45 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316736860.html), and the coalition against it is composed principally of environmental organizations and labor unions (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317611394.html).
The two sides have clashed mightily over data centers (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705781.html), which are broadly unpopular with the public and which the No campaign says could make a bid for the streamlined permitting process, something the Yes side strenuously denies.
Voters in earlier polling indicated broad support for reforming CEQA, if not necessarily for the specifics of Prop. 45. Of likely voters, 73% told PPIC this summer they’d vote yes on a proposal to modify environmental reviews for housing, transportation, health, water and clean energy projects. At the time the question did not carry the specific ballot language for the measure.
Election security
PPIC’s pollsters were calling voters amid an extraordinary period of clashes (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317690067.html) between federal and state officials over California’s election (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705634.html) security. U.S. Department of Justice attorneys sued the state in an attempt to force a review its voter rolls, and last week brought highly publicized charges against 28 California residents (https://www.sacbee.com/news/california/article317685125.html) they said voted illegally because they are not (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317689474.html) U.S. citizens. State officials have defended California’s electoral systems (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317738101.html) and accused the Trump administration of sowing doubt and chaos ahead of the midterm election.
A majority of Californians maintain confidence in the state’s ballot counting. Of likely voters, 63% have either “a great deal” or “quite a lot” of confidence in the state’s election system, according to the poll, while 15% said they had only “some confidence” and 22% said they had “very little confidence.” Seven in 10 likely voters support sending a vote-by-mail ballot to every active registered voter before each election.
Proposition 39, which is conservative Assemblymember Carl DeMaio’s answer to what he says are widespread, bipartisan concerns about the state’s election security, continued in the latest PPIC poll to be underwater, with just 41% saying they’d vote for it. Prop. 39 would require voters (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005401.html) to bring a government-issued ID to polling places or write the end of an identification number on mail ballots. It also requires county officials to scrub voter rolls for citizenship.
Loading…
As economic worries grow, Newsom’s popularity dips
Governor Newsom’s favorability ratings have dipped in the last months of his eight-year tenure as state leader. Just 47% of polled adults and 49% of likely voters told PPIC this month they approved of his job performance. It is the first time his job performance rating has dipped in the PPIC poll below 50% since last October. About 7 in 10 Democrats and 1 in 10 Republicans approve of the governor, and he is more popular in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles than elsewhere in California, PPIC found.
Newsom is widely considered to be planning a presidential bid in 2028. His dip in the polling this month seems less attributable to any new policy position or statements than to just a general gloom among California residents about the state’s direction, Baldassare said. A large majority of voters, 79% are pessimistic about the economy, around 73% say their income isn’t keeping up with inflation and 55% say the state is headed in the wrong direction.
“This is just general unhappiness,” Baldassare said. And, “what you’re seeing in our poll from that general unhappiness is now some majorities saying they disapprove of their governor and their Legislature.”

Support for billionaire tax, permitting reform measures both drop in new polling
By Andrew Graham
October 27, 2026 9:00 PM
Susan Silva fills out her ballot at the vote center at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. A new poll from the Public Policy Institute of California found just 46% of likely voters will support the billionaire’s tax.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Support for a ballot measure to tax billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317272374.html) slid six points since September as California’s ultra-wealthy class spend hundreds of millions of dollars opposing (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317386167.html) the measure, according to a newly released poll from the Public Policy Institute of California released one week before the Nov. 3 election.
The October poll found just 46% (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 40, the billionaire’s tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317075667.html), while 52% would vote no. That’s a flip from the September polling, when 52% of likely voters considered themselves a Yes vote. The latest polling was conducted from Oct. 16 to Oct. 22.
The 6% lead for the No side falls outside the poll’s margin of error, which was around 3% according to PPIC.
The decline was among the most noteworthy changes in polling about the November ballot, PPIC poll director Mark Baldassare told The Sacramento Bee. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra maintained a 24-point lead over Republican Steve Hilton (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317800503.html) in the governor’s race, up from a 22-point lead in September. A majority of voters continue to tell pollsters they’re more likely to vote for a Democrat than a Republican for the U.S. House, though the survey does not break down the state’s contested battleground district races (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317708380.html).
» Election news in your inbox: Sign up for our election newsletter here (https://www.sacbee.com/newsletters?newsletter=sacramento_election_newsletter&storylink=inline_story_link_cf)
Proposition 45 slips into minority support
Meanwhile, the split over another of the election cycle’s most contentious measures, a bid to reform permitting under (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317756293.html) the California Environmental Quality Act, remained tight. However, for the first time in PPIC’s polling the measure, Proposition 45, faces opposition from a slim majority of likely voters. Now, 50% of respondents told PPIC’s pollsters they’d vote against it, while 46% said they planned to back it and 4% remain undecided.
A month ago, 49% of likely voters said they were a yes on the measure, while 46% were a no.
Prop. 45 would impose deadlines on agencies to complete CEQA reviews and on courts to resolve lawsuits for eight categories of building projects. Proponents, which include business interests, home builders and utility companies, say it will speed projects that California communities are dying to build, but that are hampered by cost increases and delays from CEQA litigation. Opponents say it too heavily tilts the judicial and regulatory scales toward approving projects over community objections. It also gives developers a route to sue the government over project denials.
The tight margins, after campaigning by both sides, show the measure is a tricky one (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705781.html) for Californians who value environmental protections but are frustrated by the state’s high housing and utility costs, Baldassare said. In the same survey data, more than half of Californians named the cost of living, inflation and housing costs as the most important issues facing the state.
“This is a tough one for people to figure out how they should vote on this,” Baldassare said of Prop. 45. “I think it’s one of the propositions that people are most conflicted about.”
The tight polling reflects divides around the proposal that have played out in some unusual ways. Though a majority of Republican voters favors Prop. 45, 41% remain opposed in the latest PPIC poll, and some county-level Republican parties have split (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317563736.html) from the state central committee, which endorsed it. Affordable housing groups have also split over the measure, and some prominent elected Democratic officials who have called for CEQA reforms in the past, such as Gov. Gavin Newsom, have stayed on the sidelines (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317625735.html).
The California Democratic Party opposes Prop. 45 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316736860.html), and the coalition against it is composed principally of environmental organizations and labor unions (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317611394.html).
The two sides have clashed mightily over data centers (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705781.html), which are broadly unpopular with the public and which the No campaign says could make a bid for the streamlined permitting process, something the Yes side strenuously denies.
Voters in earlier polling indicated broad support for reforming CEQA, if not necessarily for the specifics of Prop. 45. Of likely voters, 73% told PPIC this summer they’d vote yes on a proposal to modify environmental reviews for housing, transportation, health, water and clean energy projects. At the time the question did not carry the specific ballot language for the measure.
Election security
PPIC’s pollsters were calling voters amid an extraordinary period of clashes (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317690067.html) between federal and state officials over California’s election (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705634.html) security. U.S. Department of Justice attorneys sued the state in an attempt to force a review its voter rolls, and last week brought highly publicized charges against 28 California residents (https://www.sacbee.com/news/california/article317685125.html) they said voted illegally because they are not (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317689474.html) U.S. citizens. State officials have defended California’s electoral systems (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317738101.html) and accused the Trump administration of sowing doubt and chaos ahead of the midterm election.
A majority of Californians maintain confidence in the state’s ballot counting. Of likely voters, 63% have either “a great deal” or “quite a lot” of confidence in the state’s election system, according to the poll, while 15% said they had only “some confidence” and 22% said they had “very little confidence.” Seven in 10 likely voters support sending a vote-by-mail ballot to every active registered voter before each election.
Proposition 39, which is conservative Assemblymember Carl DeMaio’s answer to what he says are widespread, bipartisan concerns about the state’s election security, continued in the latest PPIC poll to be underwater, with just 41% saying they’d vote for it. Prop. 39 would require voters (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005401.html) to bring a government-issued ID to polling places or write the end of an identification number on mail ballots. It also requires county officials to scrub voter rolls for citizenship.
Loading…
As economic worries grow, Newsom’s popularity dips
Governor Newsom’s favorability ratings have dipped in the last months of his eight-year tenure as state leader. Just 47% of polled adults and 49% of likely voters told PPIC this month they approved of his job performance. It is the first time his job performance rating has dipped in the PPIC poll below 50% since last October. About 7 in 10 Democrats and 1 in 10 Republicans approve of the governor, and he is more popular in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles than elsewhere in California, PPIC found.
Newsom is widely considered to be planning a presidential bid in 2028. His dip in the polling this month seems less attributable to any new policy position or statements than to just a general gloom among California residents about the state’s direction, Baldassare said. A large majority of voters, 79% are pessimistic about the economy, around 73% say their income isn’t keeping up with inflation and 55% say the state is headed in the wrong direction.
“This is just general unhappiness,” Baldassare said. And, “what you’re seeing in our poll from that general unhappiness is now some majorities saying they disapprove of their governor and their Legislature.”

Jennifer L. Hernandez | Scott Levin Gesundheit | Daniela de la Rosa
This Holland & Knight report represents the one of the most comprehensive studies of California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) appellate outcomes to date, covering 498 published and unpublished decisions from 2013 to 2023.
The study found that nearly two-thirds of challenged projects were infill development, while residential projects represented the largest category of appeals (25.5 percent) and infrastructure needed to support development was also frequently challenged.
The findings reflect a larger appellate caseload than previously recognized and point to a CEQA litigation burden that continues to delay projects for years, complicating California's efforts to expand housing and modernize critical infrastructure.
...
CEQA trial and appellate court proceedings typically take about five years to complete, and while litigation is pending, most approved projects are stalled.

Now I have a robust picture. Let me do a couple more checks:

1. The empirical evidence on CEQA's effect on housing: Rose Foundation studies show CEQA affects a small fraction of housing projects; the Holland & Knight study (Jennifer Hernandez) shows litigation disproportionately targets housing. Let me check both, especially the more recent one (Hernandez 2026 CEQA study) cited by the Yes campaign.

2. Whether there's an "affordability" mechanism — verified: none in the text.

3. Latest polling and any late-breaking news (e.g., election is Nov 3, 2026; today's date appears to be around Nov 2-3, 2026 based on Legal Planet post dated Nov 2, 2026, and SF Chronicle "Monday, November 2nd 2026").

Let me check the Hernandez 2026 CEQA study to weigh the pro-side empirical claims, and check the most recent poll (PPIC Oct 26).

Actually, let me be efficient. Key remaining questions for my decision:
- Is the "yes" case empirically sound (CEQA is a major driver of housing costs)? Evidence is mixed; the Legislature already exempted most infill housing in 2025 (AB 130), and 17,913 units have been entitled under it. So the marginal housing benefit of Prop 45 is smaller than advertised, while it also covers sprawl subdivisions, freeways, water projects, warehouses-adjacent broadband, etc.
- The measure's most troubling features (per neutral/near-neutral legal experts): (a) locks in "existing laws" as of application date, freezing environmental standards; (b) narrows judicial review to "objective existing laws" — arguably rendering CEQA's core "significant effect" analysis unenforceable; (c) courts cannot stop a project even if review was deficient (only the noncomplying part), and injunctions require "clear and convincing evidence" of a "specific, adverse impact upon public safety"; (d) one applicant-designed alternative, presumed to lessen impacts; (e) capped comment periods and exclusion of late comments from the record, plus no new comment period if the project changes in response to comments; (f) two-thirds legislative vote to amend + must "further" the chapter's purposes = effectively permanent; (g) excludes non-federally-recognized tribes from consultation (dozens of tribes, including in Bay Area, Central Coast, LA); (h) occupies the field + controls over conflicting law + frozen statutory cross-references as of Dec 31, 2025; (i) continuous general fund appropriation for independent counsel to defend it; (j) broad "essential" definitions incl. ancillary infrastructure, ambiguity re data centers/warehouses, wildfire "vegetation management" (could cover commercial logging); (k) developer right to sue agencies over denials/conditions; (l) "fullest possible weight" to approval — a pro-approval interpretive thumb on the scale.
- LAO: initial costs high tens of millions to >$100M annually; longer-term uncertain.
- Notably, the coalition is unusual: California Democratic Party, California Labor Federation, State Building & Construction Trades Council, League of Women Voters, Sierra Club, NRDC, Center for Biological Diversity, Earthjustice oppose; while business/developers/utilities/homebuilders, CA Republican Party, hospitals, water association, some affordable housing groups, LULAC, NAACP CA support. Editorial boards split: 28 newspapers Yes (incl. SD Union-Tribune, SCNG's 11 papers, McClatchy CA board incl. Sacramento Bee, Mercury News/East Bay Times); SF Chronicle No; LA Times columnist Skelton No.
- Many prominent CEQA reformers (Wiener, CA YIMBY, YIMBY Action, SPUR, Abundant Housing LA, Tom Steyer) neutral or opposed — an important signal: the people most committed to fixing CEQA don't think this is the right fix. That's a strong indicator that this measure is overbroad/poorly drafted.
- Polling: PPIC Oct 2026: 46% yes / 50% no — likely to fail or be very close.

Given the "irreversibility" (two-thirds amendment requirement, must further purposes), the interpretive thumb toward approval, the narrowing of judicial review to "objective existing laws" (which likely guts CEQA's substantive check), the freezing of standards at application date, the exclusion of non-federally recognized tribes, the continuous appropriation for private counsel, the broad and ambiguous "essential" definitions, and the fact that the Legislature has already passed targeted reforms (AB 130/SB 131) and can continue doing so — while Prop 45 would lock in a badly drafted, one-sided overhaul that can't be fixed without a two-thirds vote — I lean NO.

Counter-consideration: The genuine problem of CEQA abuse/delay is real, and the measure has some reasonable features (deadlines, one-shot completeness corrections list, 270-day judicial clock). Also there's an argument that voting No preserves a status quo that delays clean energy and housing. But the measure is an initiative statute that cannot be amended except by 2/3 vote in a direction that furthers streamlining — a huge red flag for a 41-page, complex, ambiguous law that even its supporters admit will generate litigation over its scope (data centers). And critically, the Legislature remains free to pass targeted CEQA reform after a No vote (as it has repeatedly done); a No doesn't freeze anything. Whereas a Yes locks in a pro-approval thumb and near-permanent constraints.

Also worth weighing: the fiscal cost (LAO), the removal of the court's power to halt a project pending correction of a deficient EIR — which Sivas calls rendering CEQA "a paper tiger." And the "vested rights"/existing-laws freeze which could undermine the state's ability to update environmental protections.

I'm fairly confident in NO. Also verify the claim about tribes and the two-thirds amendment.

Support for billionaire tax, permitting reform measures both drop in new polling
By Andrew Graham
October 27, 2026 9:00 PM
Susan Silva fills out her ballot at the vote center at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. A new poll from the Public Policy Institute of California found just 46% of likely voters will support the billionaire’s tax.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Support for a ballot measure to tax billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317272374.html) slid six points since September as California’s ultra-wealthy class spend hundreds of millions of dollars opposing (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317386167.html) the measure, according to a newly released poll from the Public Policy Institute of California released one week before the Nov. 3 election.
The October poll found just 46% (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 40, the billionaire’s tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317075667.html), while 52% would vote no. That’s a flip from the September polling, when 52% of likely voters considered themselves a Yes vote. The latest polling was conducted from Oct. 16 to Oct. 22.
The 6% lead for the No side falls outside the poll’s margin of error, which was around 3% according to PPIC.
The decline was among the most noteworthy changes in polling about the November ballot, PPIC poll director Mark Baldassare told The Sacramento Bee. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra maintained a 24-point lead over Republican Steve Hilton (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317800503.html) in the governor’s race, up from a 22-point lead in September. A majority of voters continue to tell pollsters they’re more likely to vote for a Democrat than a Republican for the U.S. House, though the survey does not break down the state’s contested battleground district races (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317708380.html).
» Election news in your inbox: Sign up for our election newsletter here (https://www.sacbee.com/newsletters?newsletter=sacramento_election_newsletter&storylink=inline_story_link_cf)
Proposition 45 slips into minority support
Meanwhile, the split over another of the election cycle’s most contentious measures, a bid to reform permitting under (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317756293.html) the California Environmental Quality Act, remained tight. However, for the first time in PPIC’s polling the measure, Proposition 45, faces opposition from a slim majority of likely voters. Now, 50% of respondents told PPIC’s pollsters they’d vote against it, while 46% said they planned to back it and 4% remain undecided.
A month ago, 49% of likely voters said they were a yes on the measure, while 46% were a no.
Prop. 45 would impose deadlines on agencies to complete CEQA reviews and on courts to resolve lawsuits for eight categories of building projects. Proponents, which include business interests, home builders and utility companies, say it will speed projects that California communities are dying to build, but that are hampered by cost increases and delays from CEQA litigation. Opponents say it too heavily tilts the judicial and regulatory scales toward approving projects over community objections. It also gives developers a route to sue the government over project denials.
The tight margins, after campaigning by both sides, show the measure is a tricky one (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705781.html) for Californians who value environmental protections but are frustrated by the state’s high housing and utility costs, Baldassare said. In the same survey data, more than half of Californians named the cost of living, inflation and housing costs as the most important issues facing the state.
“This is a tough one for people to figure out how they should vote on this,” Baldassare said of Prop. 45. “I think it’s one of the propositions that people are most conflicted about.”
The tight polling reflects divides around the proposal that have played out in some unusual ways. Though a majority of Republican voters favors Prop. 45, 41% remain opposed in the latest PPIC poll, and some county-level Republican parties have split (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317563736.html) from the state central committee, which endorsed it. Affordable housing groups have also split over the measure, and some prominent elected Democratic officials who have called for CEQA reforms in the past, such as Gov. Gavin Newsom, have stayed on the sidelines (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317625735.html).
The California Democratic Party opposes Prop. 45 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316736860.html), and the coalition against it is composed principally of environmental organizations and labor unions (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317611394.html).
The two sides have clashed mightily over data centers (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705781.html), which are broadly unpopular with the public and which the No campaign says could make a bid for the streamlined permitting process, something the Yes side strenuously denies.
Voters in earlier polling indicated broad support for reforming CEQA, if not necessarily for the specifics of Prop. 45. Of likely voters, 73% told PPIC this summer they’d vote yes on a proposal to modify environmental reviews for housing, transportation, health, water and clean energy projects. At the time the question did not carry the specific ballot language for the measure.
Election security
PPIC’s pollsters were calling voters amid an extraordinary period of clashes (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317690067.html) between federal and state officials over California’s election (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705634.html) security. U.S. Department of Justice attorneys sued the state in an attempt to force a review its voter rolls, and last week brought highly publicized charges against 28 California residents (https://www.sacbee.com/news/california/article317685125.html) they said voted illegally because they are not (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317689474.html) U.S. citizens. State officials have defended California’s electoral systems (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317738101.html) and accused the Trump administration of sowing doubt and chaos ahead of the midterm election.
A majority of Californians maintain confidence in the state’s ballot counting. Of likely voters, 63% have either “a great deal” or “quite a lot” of confidence in the state’s election system, according to the poll, while 15% said they had only “some confidence” and 22% said they had “very little confidence.” Seven in 10 likely voters support sending a vote-by-mail ballot to every active registered voter before each election.
Proposition 39, which is conservative Assemblymember Carl DeMaio’s answer to what he says are widespread, bipartisan concerns about the state’s election security, continued in the latest PPIC poll to be underwater, with just 41% saying they’d vote for it. Prop. 39 would require voters (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005401.html) to bring a government-issued ID to polling places or write the end of an identification number on mail ballots. It also requires county officials to scrub voter rolls for citizenship.
Loading…
As economic worries grow, Newsom’s popularity dips
Governor Newsom’s favorability ratings have dipped in the last months of his eight-year tenure as state leader. Just 47% of polled adults and 49% of likely voters told PPIC this month they approved of his job performance. It is the first time his job performance rating has dipped in the PPIC poll below 50% since last October. About 7 in 10 Democrats and 1 in 10 Republicans approve of the governor, and he is more popular in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles than elsewhere in California, PPIC found.
Newsom is widely considered to be planning a presidential bid in 2028. His dip in the polling this month seems less attributable to any new policy position or statements than to just a general gloom among California residents about the state’s direction, Baldassare said. A large majority of voters, 79% are pessimistic about the economy, around 73% say their income isn’t keeping up with inflation and 55% say the state is headed in the wrong direction.
“This is just general unhappiness,” Baldassare said. And, “what you’re seeing in our poll from that general unhappiness is now some majorities saying they disapprove of their governor and their Legislature.”
