“Prop 45 will modernize the approval process for essential projects by establishing clear, enforceable timelines for agency decisions and court challenges,” the chamber said in promotional materials, “while keeping environmental protections intact and preserving worker protections, tribal protections and local control.”
Critics say Prop 45 will gut the state’s primary vehicle for allowing people to learn about plans for polluting developments in their neighborhoods and propose alternatives.
“It undermines basically every stage of that process,” said Woody Little, the spokesperson for No on Prop 45.
Little and his allies say the 41-page ballot measure (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) was written by corporations who have paid to get their special interests on the ballot to create loopholes that favor polluting industries like recently regulated (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2026/09/21/governor-newsom-signs-most-comprehensive-data-center-laws-in-the-nation-providing-communities-more-control-on-water-electricity-and-land-use/) data centers while limiting the input of communities and local tribes.
Critics of CEQA, signed in 1970 by then-Gov. Ronald Reagan, blame the law for hobbling home construction and driving housing and cost of living increases in California, which are among the highest in the nation.
Prop 45 will lower housing and utility costs by reducing “endless” bureaucratic delays and protect taxpayers by reducing waste and cost overruns, Yes on Prop 45 materials argue.
Yet there is no requirement in the measure to reduce housing costs or utility bills. And the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=45&year=2026) estimates that Prop 45 could leave state and local governments paying $100 million or more a year, partly to cover fast-tracked projects’ environmental impacts.
“The housing issue is a smokescreen for all these other polluting projects,” said Little.
California passed laws last year that significantly streamlined CEQA by exempting (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB130) urban and mixed-use housing construction from its provisions as well as certain infrastructure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB131) and clean energy (https://www.energy.ca.gov/programs-and-topics/topics/power-plants/opt-certification-program) projects.
“ I would hope that 100 percent of Californians would see this radical reshaping of California’s environmental law for the dangerous thing that it is. A wolf in sheep’s clothing.”
— Woody Little, No on Prop 45
None of the grassroots groups that promote “yes in my backyard,” or YIMBY (https://yimbyaction.org/), policies to build more housing and public transit in urban and suburban areas support Prop 45, Little said. Most are neutral, he said, while others oppose it.
Expanding housing beyond already developed areas means building new freeways, water connections and other expensive infrastructure that taxpayers ultimately pay for, Little said. And these projects often encroach on the wildland-urban interface, raising wildfire risk just as climate change is making fires more destructive.
At a time when California is already seeing the catastrophic costs of climate-fueled fires, Little said, the state should be requiring more environmental review around developments to assess and mitigate risk, not less.
What’s “Essential”?
Prop 45 covers nine types of “essential” projects, among them housing, water systems, clean energy (including carbon capture and storage), transportation, wildfire risk reduction and broadband internet access. All related and “ancillary” infrastructure is also covered.
Whether “ancillary” includes data centers, which typically require broadband infrastructure (https://tiaonline.org/how-broadband-workforce-development-and-standards-drive-data-center-growth/), has been a major point of contention.
Prop 45’s proponents have insisted the measure does not cover data centers, but legal experts disagree, pointing to $2 million in donations from just three data center builders and language buried in the measure’s 41 pages. Eligible projects include “broadband internet access projects,” defined as “mass-market retail service … that provides the capability to transmit data to, and receive data from, all or substantially all Internet endpoints,” a recent analysis (https://www.dailyjournal.com/articles/394431-prop-45-will-speed-data-center-construction) found.

That definition includes facilities that house the physical infrastructure used to transmit consumer data to and from the internet—which describes many data centers.
Yet data centers are conspicuously absent from the list of excluded controversial projects, which includes high-speed rail, the Delta Conveyance Project (https://www.deltaconveyanceproject.com/about-the-delta-conveyance-project), nuclear power and oil and gas facilities.
Inside Climate News asked the Yes on Prop 45 campaign why it sought to further limit environmental review after California had already significantly streamlined CEQA and why the measure does not explicitly exclude data centers. The campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
California Resources Corp., the state’s largest (https://www.crc.com/news-releases/news-release-details/california-resources-corporation-completes-acquisition-crimson) oil and gas producer, has donated $500,000 directly to Prop 45 campaigns and another $500,000 (https://cal-access.sos.ca.gov/Campaign/Committees/Detail.aspx?id=1021742&session=2025&view=received) to a business committee sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce. Oil and gas facilities are explicitly excluded from Prop 45, but CRC has a data center under environmental review at its Elk Hills oil field.
CRC did not respond to questions about whether it supports Prop 45 in order to fast-track its data center application.
Protecting Community Voices
“Proposition 45 would weaken CEQA protections for the very projects that still warrant careful scrutiny—development that could put people in harm’s way, fragment wildlife habitat, threaten water resources or damage irreplaceable cultural and sacred sites,” environmental and conservation leaders argued in a recent op-ed (https://lookout.co/california-has-already-streamlined-ceqa-proposition-45-goes-too-far/story).
One of the op-ed authors, Chris Wilmers, tracks mountain lions as lead researcher for the Santa Cruz Puma Project. In his study area, retaliatory killings for preying on domestic animals and vehicle strikes are the biggest threat (https://lookout.co/mountain-lions-ucsc-researcher-chris-wilmers-on-how-new-highway-17-animal-crossing-protects-santa-cruz-mountain-lions/story) to mountain lions as new housing and roads continue to encroach on the wide-ranging carnivores’ critical habitat.
An adult male mountain lion travels through a tunnel under Highway 101, heading south toward California’s Santa Monica Mountains in 2018. Credit: National Parks Service
CEQA requires developers to weigh alternatives to mitigate harm if new evidence emerges that a project would degrade critical wildlife corridors or endangered species’ habitat. But such facts would never come to light under Prop 45, which lets developers write their own rules, Wilmers and others say.
And the ballot measure strips away the rights of tribes that aren’t recognized by the federal government to safeguard their sacred lands.
That leaves large swaths of California, including the Central Coast, the San Francisco Bay Area and much of the Los Angeles area, without any tribal representation, said Noelle Chambers, executive director of the Amah Mutsun Land Trust.
Ethnographic studies conducted through CEQA consultations allowed the Amah Mutsun Tribal Band to protect burial grounds, artifacts and other sacred sites by stopping a proposed sand and gravel mine (https://openspacetrust.org/blog/sargent-ranch/) near Gilroy.
Prop 45 creates a “really harmful” legal precedent in the state by excluding non-federally recognized tribes from the process, Chambers said.
Julia Stein, deputy director of the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment at the University of California, Los Angeles, calls Prop 45 “a blunt force instrument” that is unlikely to build more projects faster by removing public participation.
It will cause a real loss of community engagement, she said, noting that CEQA is the only avenue for environmental justice communities to influence the environmental impacts of projects in their neighborhoods.
“We lived through a big infrastructure build-out in this country without laws like CEQA in the 1950s and ’60s, and we got environmental justice communities right next to freeways as a result,” Stein said.
CEQA has helped many communities (https://www.phi.org/thought-leadership/act-on-climate-california-communities-addressing-climate-change-and-health/) with elevated rates of asthma, cancer, heart disease and other ailments linked to industrial pollution limit additional harms in their neighborhoods.
A historically overburdened Latino community in southeast Los Angeles used a court order to compel a local government (https://legal-planet.org/2022/02/23/why-ceqa-is-a-useful-tool-for-environmental-justice-communities-in-california/) to review the risks of building an elementary school on a site contaminated with arsenic, and likely lead and asbestos, and require a cleanup. The mostly Latino residents of Riverside County’s Moreno Valley won an agreement to mitigate the harms (https://biologicaldiversity.org/programs/energy-justice/pdfs/WorldLogisticsCenter-Settlement-Agreement-20210429.pdf) on local air quality, climate and wildlife created by heavy-duty trucks serving a 40-million-square-foot warehouse.
Such mitigating measures might never have been identified, let alone required, if Prop 45 had been in effect, opponents say.
In addition to reducing the timeline for public agencies to review projects and fundamentally changing who can provide input, Prop 45 says only the developer or corporation can propose alternatives, said Mabel Tsang, political director for the California Environmental Justice Alliance, which opposes Prop 45.
“That takes away the strongest tool that communities like ours can use to protect ourselves from the worst health impacts before another polluting project is approved next door to our homes,” Tsang said.
Reagan, who signed CEQA as California governor but was known for accelerating deregulation as president, saw environmental protection as a nonpartisan issue. “Preservation of our environment is not a liberal or conservative challenge, it’s common sense,” he said during his 1984 State of the Union (https://www.reaganlibrary.gov/archives/speech/address-joint-session-congress-state-union-january-1984) address.
Now, on the heels of the Trump administration’s attempts to roll back the nation’s major environmental laws, experts say CEQA is more important than ever to safeguard public health and the environment from polluting industries.
Recent polling suggests that on Nov. 3, voters may not approve a measure designed to kneecap California’s most important air- and water-quality protection law.
A poll released Tuesday (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) by the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California shows that 50 percent of voters oppose Prop 45, while those who support it dropped to 46 percent from 73 percent in July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/), when voters knew only general information about the proposition.

Proposition 45
Speed up environmental reviews for housing and infrastructure
Proposition 45 would limit reviews under the state’s landmark environmental law, the California Environmental Quality Act. Placed on the ballot by the California Chamber of Commerce, the measure aims to help developers advance projects they designate as “essential” more quickly and easily. It would impose a 365-day limit on environmental reviews for those projects, including infrastructure like roads and bridges, housing, schools, broadband and wildfire mitigation. It would also require courts to rule within 270 days on lawsuits related to the environmental review law.

Summary
Support
The California Chamber of Commerce says the state’s environmental review law is outdated and creates expensive bureaucracy and frivolous litigation that slows development. It argues that delays in reviewing projects ultimately increase costs that are passed down to taxpayers and consumers. The group argues the measure will speed up development while keeping essential environmental protections in place.
Oppose
Opponents say the measure would weaken California’s environmental review law, which exists to protect people and the environment from potentially harmful developments. They say Proposition 45 would strip agencies of the tools they have to protect communities, increase costly litigation and practically eliminate their ability to enforce the law. 1. Newsom decries ‘weaponization' of environmental law, but stays silent on Prop. 45
https://www.sanluisobispo.com/news/california/article317625735.html
At an economic forum Wednesday, Gov.
Gavin Newsom touted changes to the California Environmental Quality Act that he strong-armed through the Legislature last year.
But he said the law's 'weaponization' still delays much-needed building projects.
...
The comments stood in stark relief to his silence on Proposition 45, perhaps the most significant CEQA reform effort on the table yet.
Clean energy infrastructure like solar installations and battery storage facilities are among the projects that would receive shortened timelines under the measure.
...
Prop.
45 is one of two the governor has stayed silent on, despite his vocal CEQA reform push.
The ballot measure did not come up at Wednesday's discussion, a livestreamed conversation with his former economic advisor, Lenny Mendonca.
...
Last week, a spokesperson for Newsom said he was still reviewing Prop.
45. On Wednesday, his office did not respond to a request for comment on his disposition toward the measure.
...
Newsom hoped his likely predecessor, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra, continued to push permitting reforms through the California Legislature, he told the California Economic Summit crowd.
...
'And I think he has a Legislature right now that's ready for that.'

Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects. Initiative Statute.” (Attorney General title and summary, December 26, 2025)
Measure’s own name: The Building an Affordable California Act (AG No. 25-0023A1)
Type: Initiated state statute
A vote YES means: A new “essential projects” category (most housing, water, clean energy, medical, public safety, broadband, and transportation projects) gets hard deadlines for CEQA review, a slimmed-down alternatives analysis, and tighter limits on lawsuits, all written into the Public Resources Code [1, Sec. 21013].
A vote NO means: CEQA’s existing review timelines, alternatives requirements, and judicial-review rules stay in place for these projects.
Sponsor/proponent: California Chamber of Commerce. Proponent of record: Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer LLP.
On the ballot because: Qualified by random-sample signature check on June 16, 2026, and certified eligible June 25, 2026. The measure needed 546,651 valid signatures.
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf)
LAO analysis: Ballot analysis of Initiative 25-0023 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-023)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 45 would carve a new fast-track lane through the California Environmental Quality Act for what it calls “essential projects.” It adds a new chapter, Chapter 1.5, to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code, the part of state law that is CEQA. It does not repeal CEQA, and it does not touch the other environmental statutes it names, such as the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the California Coastal Act. What it changes is CEQA’s procedure for a defined set of projects [1, Sec. 1 (21011(h)), 21012-21033].
The measure does three main things for essential projects. First, it puts public agencies on a clock. An agency has thirty days to decide whether an application is complete or the application is deemed complete automatically. Once complete, a lead agency has 365 days to decide whether to certify an environmental impact report (EIR), 180 days to act on a negative declaration, and 90 days to document an exemption. For the 365-day and 90-day review clocks the measure counts only business days, not weekends or state holidays, so the real-world calendar is longer than the raw numbers suggest [1, Secs. 21017-21019, 21028(c)].
Second, it shrinks the alternatives analysis. Today a CEQA environmental impact report must study a reasonable range of alternatives to a project. Under Proposition 45, an EIR for an essential project needs to analyze only the project itself, one alternative developed by the applicant, and the “no project” alternative. The measure declares that any additional alternatives are “unnecessary” and that no agency may require them [1, Sec. 21025].
Third, it narrows the courtroom. A challenger must sue within thirty days of the agency’s notice of determination, the case must finish within 270 days including any appeal, and the court must use the deferential substantial-evidence standard rather than independent judgment. A court that finds a defect may order the agency to redo only the specific study at issue. It “may not order or direct” the agency to rescind its approval of the project, and once a project clears review its later construction and implementation approvals cannot be challenged again [1, Secs. 21026-21027].
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0023A1, “Building an Affordable California Act,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0023A1%20%28%26quot%3BEssential%20Projects%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (amended language submitted November 24, 2025)
Key language:
“‘Essential project’ means a project that meets all of the following requirements … The project does not include a jail or other detention facility, or involve the development of a new oil or natural gas production facility.” [1, Sec. 21028(h)]
“A court may not order or direct via writ or any other form of order, injunction, or decision that an agency rescind its approval of the essential project.” [1, Sec. 21027(d)]
What it amends: Adds Chapter 1.5 (commencing with Section 21010) to Division 13 of the Public Resources Code. Because it is an initiative statute rather than a constitutional amendment, the legislature could later amend it, but only in ways that further the measure’s purposes unless it says otherwise. The measure also adds a self-defense clause. If the governor and attorney general both decline to defend it in court, the attorney general must appoint independent counsel, funded by a continuous general fund appropriation [1, Secs. 21010, Section 4].
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who? Sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce, with the initiative filed by attorney Kurt R. Oneto of Nielsen Merksamer. Supporters include the California Building Industry Association, the California Hospital Association, NAACP California, and Pacific Gas and Electric. Opposition is led by environmental organizations, including Sierra Club California, the Planning and Conservation League, and CalBike.
What? A new “essential projects” category covering most housing, water, clean energy, medical, public-safety, broadband, and transportation projects, given fixed review deadlines, a one-alternative EIR, and tighter judicial review. Jails and detention facilities and new oil and gas production facilities are excluded, and by definition Delta conveyance and high-speed rail are left out of the water and transportation categories. [1, Secs. 21013, 21028].
Where? Statewide, applied to all public agencies and written into the Public Resources Code [1, Sec. 21014(d)].
When? On the November 3, 2026, ballot. It takes effect the day after the election if it passes and applies to applications deemed complete after that date, including projects that withdraw and resubmit to opt in [1, Secs. 21014(f)-(g), 21033].
Why? The proponents frame CEQA delay and litigation as a driver of California’s high housing, energy, and infrastructure costs. Their stated purpose is to “make California more affordable by streamlining and speeding up approval of essential projects” while keeping the state’s other environmental laws intact [1, Secs. 21011-21012].
4. Trade-offs
CEQA review and the lawsuits that follow can add years and cost to housing and infrastructure, and the delay is not evenly aimed at the most polluting projects. The legislature itself has spent recent sessions passing narrower CEQA exemptions for infill housing and other priorities, which shows that the cost-of-building concern is bipartisan and real, not manufactured. Proposition 45 is the broadest response yet because it does by initiative, and across seven whole project categories, what the legislature has done piecemeal.
Every lever the measure pulls to go faster also removes a check that CEQA built in on purpose. Hard deadlines with a “deemed complete” default speed things up, and they also let a clock, rather than a finished analysis, decide when review ends. A one-alternative EIR is cheaper and quicker, and it also means the public document may never study the option that would have reduced harm the most. The substantial-evidence standard and the bar on rescinding approvals cut litigation risk for builders, and they also make it harder for a neighbor or a tribe to stop a project that was genuinely under-analyzed. None of these is a free lunch. Each is a real gain in speed bought with a real reduction in review.
Two things keep this from being a simple pro-building versus pro-environment fight. First, the measure leaves the substantive environmental statutes standing. A project that violates the Clean Water Act or the Endangered Species Act is still illegal under those laws. What changes is CEQA’s procedural review, which is disclosure and analysis, not the pollution limits themselves. Second, the fight will be about the word “essential.” The definitions are broad. “Essential clean energy” reaches carbon-capture and hydrogen infrastructure, and the categories sweep in “related and ancillary” infrastructure as part of the “whole of the project.” How wide that lane runs, and how much of California’s building actually qualifies, is the question the ballot label cannot answer [1, Secs. 21028(f), (h)].
Many CEQA issues are not about acceptable levels of environmental damage. Instead, project opponents use procedural complaints under CEQA to slow down projects that they dislike for reasons having nothing to do with the environment. The proposition’s backers wish to reduce the use of CEQA for such purposes.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
It replaces open-ended CEQA timelines with firm deadlines, which can cut the years of delay that raise the cost of housing, water, clean energy, and hospitals [1, Secs. 21018-21019].
The streamlined one-alternative EIR reduces the cost and length of environmental review while still requiring a “no project” comparison [1, Sec. 21025].
Tighter judicial rules, a 270-day case clock, and a bar on rescinding approvals reduce the litigation risk that can stall financing on approved projects [1, Secs. 21026-21027].
The LAO expects state and local governments to see long-run net savings from reduced administrative and legal workload once the system is running.
It leaves the underlying pollution-control statutes—the Clean Water Act, Clean Air Act, Endangered Species Act, and Coastal Act—in force, so it narrows CEQA procedure rather than repealing environmental protection [1, Sec. 21011(h)].
Potential risks
A one-alternative EIR and a “deemed complete” default can end review before the analysis is finished, so real environmental or community harms may go unstudied [1, Secs. 21017, 21025].
The bar on rescinding an approval and on challenging later construction approvals sharply limits the public’s ability to stop an under-reviewed project [1, Sec. 21027(d)-(e)].
The “essential project” definitions are broad and include ancillary infrastructure, so fights over what qualifies will be frequent and consequential [1, Sec. 21028(h)].
The LAO estimates implementation costs in the tens of millions of dollars annually for the first several years, with uncertain long-run court effects that could run from savings to added costs.
The self-defense clause commits an open-ended general fund appropriation to hired outside counsel if state officials decline to defend the measure [1, Section 4].
6. Open questions
How much of California’s actual building pipeline meets the “essential project” definition once ancillary infrastructure and the seven categories are counted?
Will the 365 business-day and 90 business-day clocks, which run longer than calendar deadlines, deliver the speed proponents promise?
Does limiting an EIR to one applicant-designed alternative meaningfully weaken the document’s ability to surface lower-impact options?
How will courts read “objective, quantifiable, and written standards” as the new test for a valid CEQA challenge, and how many suits does that screen out?
If the measure passes, how much litigation will target the boundaries of the definitions themselves, and who pays for the state’s defense under the independent-counsel clause?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
CEQA delay is a real driver of what it costs to build housing, water projects, and energy capacity in California. Proposition 45 speeds up those projects by shortening deadlines, shrinking the alternatives study, and limiting lawsuits. The questions are whether faster building is worth a lighter environmental and public review and whether to trust the broad definition of “essential” to stay in its lane.
Every provision that makes a project go faster also removes a check that CEQA put there on purpose. Which risk weighs more: a needed project stalled for years by process and litigation or a harmful project approved before the harm was fully studied?

Opinion: Prop. 45 will take a meat axe to California environmental
protections
Date: October 26, 2026
Source: East Bay Times: Web Edition Articles (CA)
Section: Commentary
Author: Deborah A Sivas
Word Count: 692
However well-intentioned, support for Proposition 45 is deeply misguided. It is true that California, like most states, needs
to build more housing, renewable energy projects, and other 21st century infrastructure. But eviscerating the California
Environmental Quality Act won't do that.
At its core, CEQA is a "stop, look, and listen" law. It requires government officials to make informed decisions by
considering the environmental impacts of projects, evaluating less impactful alternatives and other ways to mitigate
adverse effects, and soliciting public input from affected communities. CEQA itself cannot prevent projects from going
forward, but it can make developers and agencies think harder about designing them in the most sustainable way.
Since CEQA's passage more than 50 years ago, developers have been trying to kill it. Their efforts have recently gained
momentum as the "Abundance" narrative has taken hold. The general concept, as the best-seller of the same name tells
us, is to rid public decisions of "paperwork and procedure and hearings and disclosure demands and lawsuits" — the very
public process innovations that have made government more accountable to constituents and significantly reduced air
and water pollution.
The California Legislature has already responded to industry concerns over project delays, repeatedly tinkering with
CEQA's provisions to help expedite the review process. The most significant of these amendments came in June 2025,
with passage of AB 130 and SB 131. These new laws exempt most urban housing from CEQA altogether and streamline
the review process for many other projects.
Developers are not content to let these substantial CEQA reforms play out. Instead, they have taken advantage of the
"Abundance" movement with an industry-funded voter initiative that goes far beyond streamlining. Proposition 45 would,
among other things, give developers new litigation rights to sue local agencies over even shorter approval deadlines,
allow developers to replace the normal "reasonable range of alternatives" that officials must consider with a single,
developer-designed onsite "alternative," and reduce the ability of the public to comment on projects.
Most troubling, Proposition 45 so severely constrains judicial review as to make CEQA meaningless. Courts finding an
environmental analysis legally deficient could not prevent the project from going forward while the CEQA flaws are
remedied. That is, the developer could build the project before the impacts are properly evaluated. This single provision
renders CEQA nothing more than a paper tiger.
And here's the kicker: If passed, Proposition 45 would prohibit future statutory amendments unless they (1) affirmatively
"further" the newly-declared statutory purpose of "streamlining and speeding approval of essential projects" and (2) are
enacted by a two-thirds vote of the Legislature. In short, developers want to disenfranchise communities in perpetuity.
The non-profit Rose Foundation has published several empirical studies (in 2016, 2021, and 2023) confirming that CEQA
affects only a very small fraction of housing projects. These studies refute the methodology and conclusions advanced in
a 2017 report by the industry's favorite private law firm.
The reasons for project delays are myriad — misaligned financial incentives, skilled labor shortages, outdated building
codes, vocal public opposition, and yes, occasionally CEQA lawsuits. The Legislature has steadily addressed these
obstacles in targeted reforms, especially with respect to housing. Instead of a surgical scalpel, Prop 45 takes a meat axe
to the law. That is likely why even the very pro-housing YIMBY movement takes no position on the initiative and why most
environmental groups and many local officials strongly oppose it.
CEQA promotes decision transparency, agency accountability, and public participation. It has significantly reduced
pollution and unsustainable resource exploitation. And it is virtually the only tool available to communities facing public
health and environmental impacts from sprawling projects like data centers, Amazon warehouses, and expanding oil
fields. Proposition 45 attempts to deprive Californians of a meaningful say in their own future, while doing nothing to make
housing more affordable or available.
Deborah A. Sivas is a professor of environmental law at Stanford Law and of environmental social science at the Doerr
School of Sustainability.

signs two bills Monday June 30, 2025 to reform CEQA, the California Environmental Quality Act, with the goal of building
housing and other projects faster. (Photo: Governor's Office)n

Now I have a robust picture. Let me do a couple more checks:

1. The empirical evidence on CEQA's effect on housing: Rose Foundation studies show CEQA affects a small fraction of housing projects; the Holland & Knight study (Jennifer Hernandez) shows litigation disproportionately targets housing. Let me check both, especially the more recent one (Hernandez 2026 CEQA study) cited by the Yes campaign.

2. Whether there's an "affordability" mechanism — verified: none in the text.

3. Latest polling and any late-breaking news (e.g., election is Nov 3, 2026; today's date appears to be around Nov 2-3, 2026 based on Legal Planet post dated Nov 2, 2026, and SF Chronicle "Monday, November 2nd 2026").

Let me check the Hernandez 2026 CEQA study to weigh the pro-side empirical claims, and check the most recent poll (PPIC Oct 26).

Actually, let me be efficient. Key remaining questions for my decision:
- Is the "yes" case empirically sound (CEQA is a major driver of housing costs)? Evidence is mixed; the Legislature already exempted most infill housing in 2025 (AB 130), and 17,913 units have been entitled under it. So the marginal housing benefit of Prop 45 is smaller than advertised, while it also covers sprawl subdivisions, freeways, water projects, warehouses-adjacent broadband, etc.
- The measure's most troubling features (per neutral/near-neutral legal experts): (a) locks in "existing laws" as of application date, freezing environmental standards; (b) narrows judicial review to "objective existing laws" — arguably rendering CEQA's core "significant effect" analysis unenforceable; (c) courts cannot stop a project even if review was deficient (only the noncomplying part), and injunctions require "clear and convincing evidence" of a "specific, adverse impact upon public safety"; (d) one applicant-designed alternative, presumed to lessen impacts; (e) capped comment periods and exclusion of late comments from the record, plus no new comment period if the project changes in response to comments; (f) two-thirds legislative vote to amend + must "further" the chapter's purposes = effectively permanent; (g) excludes non-federally-recognized tribes from consultation (dozens of tribes, including in Bay Area, Central Coast, LA); (h) occupies the field + controls over conflicting law + frozen statutory cross-references as of Dec 31, 2025; (i) continuous general fund appropriation for independent counsel to defend it; (j) broad "essential" definitions incl. ancillary infrastructure, ambiguity re data centers/warehouses, wildfire "vegetation management" (could cover commercial logging); (k) developer right to sue agencies over denials/conditions; (l) "fullest possible weight" to approval — a pro-approval interpretive thumb on the scale.
- LAO: initial costs high tens of millions to >$100M annually; longer-term uncertain.
- Notably, the coalition is unusual: California Democratic Party, California Labor Federation, State Building & Construction Trades Council, League of Women Voters, Sierra Club, NRDC, Center for Biological Diversity, Earthjustice oppose; while business/developers/utilities/homebuilders, CA Republican Party, hospitals, water association, some affordable housing groups, LULAC, NAACP CA support. Editorial boards split: 28 newspapers Yes (incl. SD Union-Tribune, SCNG's 11 papers, McClatchy CA board incl. Sacramento Bee, Mercury News/East Bay Times); SF Chronicle No; LA Times columnist Skelton No.
- Many prominent CEQA reformers (Wiener, CA YIMBY, YIMBY Action, SPUR, Abundant Housing LA, Tom Steyer) neutral or opposed — an important signal: the people most committed to fixing CEQA don't think this is the right fix. That's a strong indicator that this measure is overbroad/poorly drafted.
- Polling: PPIC Oct 2026: 46% yes / 50% no — likely to fail or be very close.

Given the "irreversibility" (two-thirds amendment requirement, must further purposes), the interpretive thumb toward approval, the narrowing of judicial review to "objective existing laws" (which likely guts CEQA's substantive check), the freezing of standards at application date, the exclusion of non-federally recognized tribes, the continuous appropriation for private counsel, the broad and ambiguous "essential" definitions, and the fact that the Legislature has already passed targeted reforms (AB 130/SB 131) and can continue doing so — while Prop 45 would lock in a badly drafted, one-sided overhaul that can't be fixed without a two-thirds vote — I lean NO.

Counter-consideration: The genuine problem of CEQA abuse/delay is real, and the measure has some reasonable features (deadlines, one-shot completeness corrections list, 270-day judicial clock). Also there's an argument that voting No preserves a status quo that delays clean energy and housing. But the measure is an initiative statute that cannot be amended except by 2/3 vote in a direction that furthers streamlining — a huge red flag for a 41-page, complex, ambiguous law that even its supporters admit will generate litigation over its scope (data centers). And critically, the Legislature remains free to pass targeted CEQA reform after a No vote (as it has repeatedly done); a No doesn't freeze anything. Whereas a Yes locks in a pro-approval thumb and near-permanent constraints.

Also worth weighing: the fiscal cost (LAO), the removal of the court's power to halt a project pending correction of a deficient EIR — which Sivas calls rendering CEQA "a paper tiger." And the "vested rights"/existing-laws freeze which could undermine the state's ability to update environmental protections.

I'm fairly confident in NO. Let me do one more verification pass: check the Hernandez 2026 CEQA study claims and the most recent poll, and see if anything changed at the last minute (e.g., a major endorsement shift, or a legal ruling). Also verify the claim about tribes and the two-thirds amendment.

Support for billionaire tax, permitting reform measures both drop in new polling
By Andrew Graham
October 27, 2026 9:00 PM
Susan Silva fills out her ballot at the vote center at the Placer County Clerk-Recorder-Elections Office in Rocklin on Tuesday, Oct. 28, 2025. A new poll from the Public Policy Institute of California found just 46% of likely voters will support the billionaire’s tax.
JOSÉ LUIS VILLEGAS
jvillegas@sacbee.com
Support for a ballot measure to tax billionaires (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317272374.html) slid six points since September as California’s ultra-wealthy class spend hundreds of millions of dollars opposing (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317386167.html) the measure, according to a newly released poll from the Public Policy Institute of California released one week before the Nov. 3 election.
The October poll found just 46% (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/) of likely voters would vote yes on Proposition 40, the billionaire’s tax (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317075667.html), while 52% would vote no. That’s a flip from the September polling, when 52% of likely voters considered themselves a Yes vote. The latest polling was conducted from Oct. 16 to Oct. 22.
The 6% lead for the No side falls outside the poll’s margin of error, which was around 3% according to PPIC.
The decline was among the most noteworthy changes in polling about the November ballot, PPIC poll director Mark Baldassare told The Sacramento Bee. Democratic gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra maintained a 24-point lead over Republican Steve Hilton (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317800503.html) in the governor’s race, up from a 22-point lead in September. A majority of voters continue to tell pollsters they’re more likely to vote for a Democrat than a Republican for the U.S. House, though the survey does not break down the state’s contested battleground district races (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317708380.html).
» Election news in your inbox: Sign up for our election newsletter here (https://www.sacbee.com/newsletters?newsletter=sacramento_election_newsletter&storylink=inline_story_link_cf)
Proposition 45 slips into minority support
Meanwhile, the split over another of the election cycle’s most contentious measures, a bid to reform permitting under (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/article317756293.html) the California Environmental Quality Act, remained tight. However, for the first time in PPIC’s polling the measure, Proposition 45, faces opposition from a slim majority of likely voters. Now, 50% of respondents told PPIC’s pollsters they’d vote against it, while 46% said they planned to back it and 4% remain undecided.
A month ago, 49% of likely voters said they were a yes on the measure, while 46% were a no.
Prop. 45 would impose deadlines on agencies to complete CEQA reviews and on courts to resolve lawsuits for eight categories of building projects. Proponents, which include business interests, home builders and utility companies, say it will speed projects that California communities are dying to build, but that are hampered by cost increases and delays from CEQA litigation. Opponents say it too heavily tilts the judicial and regulatory scales toward approving projects over community objections. It also gives developers a route to sue the government over project denials.
The tight margins, after campaigning by both sides, show the measure is a tricky one (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705781.html) for Californians who value environmental protections but are frustrated by the state’s high housing and utility costs, Baldassare said. In the same survey data, more than half of Californians named the cost of living, inflation and housing costs as the most important issues facing the state.
“This is a tough one for people to figure out how they should vote on this,” Baldassare said of Prop. 45. “I think it’s one of the propositions that people are most conflicted about.”
The tight polling reflects divides around the proposal that have played out in some unusual ways. Though a majority of Republican voters favors Prop. 45, 41% remain opposed in the latest PPIC poll, and some county-level Republican parties have split (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317563736.html) from the state central committee, which endorsed it. Affordable housing groups have also split over the measure, and some prominent elected Democratic officials who have called for CEQA reforms in the past, such as Gov. Gavin Newsom, have stayed on the sidelines (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317625735.html).
The California Democratic Party opposes Prop. 45 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article316736860.html), and the coalition against it is composed principally of environmental organizations and labor unions (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317611394.html).
The two sides have clashed mightily over data centers (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705781.html), which are broadly unpopular with the public and which the No campaign says could make a bid for the streamlined permitting process, something the Yes side strenuously denies.
Voters in earlier polling indicated broad support for reforming CEQA, if not necessarily for the specifics of Prop. 45. Of likely voters, 73% told PPIC this summer they’d vote yes on a proposal to modify environmental reviews for housing, transportation, health, water and clean energy projects. At the time the question did not carry the specific ballot language for the measure.
Election security
PPIC’s pollsters were calling voters amid an extraordinary period of clashes (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317690067.html) between federal and state officials over California’s election (https://www.sacbee.com/latest-news/article317705634.html) security. U.S. Department of Justice attorneys sued the state in an attempt to force a review its voter rolls, and last week brought highly publicized charges against 28 California residents (https://www.sacbee.com/news/california/article317685125.html) they said voted illegally because they are not (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317689474.html) U.S. citizens. State officials have defended California’s electoral systems (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317738101.html) and accused the Trump administration of sowing doubt and chaos ahead of the midterm election.
A majority of Californians maintain confidence in the state’s ballot counting. Of likely voters, 63% have either “a great deal” or “quite a lot” of confidence in the state’s election system, according to the poll, while 15% said they had only “some confidence” and 22% said they had “very little confidence.” Seven in 10 likely voters support sending a vote-by-mail ballot to every active registered voter before each election.
Proposition 39, which is conservative Assemblymember Carl DeMaio’s answer to what he says are widespread, bipartisan concerns about the state’s election security, continued in the latest PPIC poll to be underwater, with just 41% saying they’d vote for it. Prop. 39 would require voters (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317005401.html) to bring a government-issued ID to polling places or write the end of an identification number on mail ballots. It also requires county officials to scrub voter rolls for citizenship.
Loading…
As economic worries grow, Newsom’s popularity dips
Governor Newsom’s favorability ratings have dipped in the last months of his eight-year tenure as state leader. Just 47% of polled adults and 49% of likely voters told PPIC this month they approved of his job performance. It is the first time his job performance rating has dipped in the PPIC poll below 50% since last October. About 7 in 10 Democrats and 1 in 10 Republicans approve of the governor, and he is more popular in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles than elsewhere in California, PPIC found.
Newsom is widely considered to be planning a presidential bid in 2028. His dip in the polling this month seems less attributable to any new policy position or statements than to just a general gloom among California residents about the state’s direction, Baldassare said. A large majority of voters, 79% are pessimistic about the economy, around 73% say their income isn’t keeping up with inflation and 55% say the state is headed in the wrong direction.
“This is just general unhappiness,” Baldassare said. And, “what you’re seeing in our poll from that general unhappiness is now some majorities saying they disapprove of their governor and their Legislature.”

wage/skilled-workforce labor standards in place. Because nearly half of all CEQA lawsuits target

addresses fall disproportionately on public budgets. The nonpartisan LAO concludes the measure
would likely produce net savings for state and local governments over the long term and could
increase state and local tax revenue through faster project completion.
Title: Proposition 45, Building an Affordable California Act (Affordable CA). Official ballot
title: “Modifies environmental review for certain projects.”
Type: Statewide Statutory Initiative
Vote: November 2026 Statewide General Election
Status: Qualified for the November 2026 ballot by the California Secretary of State on June
16, 2026, after exceeding the 601,317-signature random-sample threshold (546,651 valid
signatures required).
Description: Reform of the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) review and
permitting process for designated essential projects.
Fiscal Impact: Legislative Analyst’s Office official fiscal impact statement issued at
qualification (June 2026): “State and local government implementation costs in the tens of
millions of dollars annually for the first several years. Over the long term, the annual net fiscal
effects are uncertain, but state and local governments likely would experience net savings due
to reduced administrative and legal workload. Net fiscal effects on state trial courts ranging
from annual savings of up to the tens of millions of dollars to annual costs of up to the low tens
of millions of dollars.”
Background
The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) is a state law enacted in 1970 which requires
local and state public agencies to assess and publicly disclose the environmental impacts of
proposed land development projects, and develop mitigation measures for those impacts in order
to secure project approval. The basic goal of CEQA is to prevent undue damage to the
SDtaxpayers.org • 2
environment and ensure the general public is informed in cases where there will be impacts to
the environment, while providing opportunities for the public to raise concerns and provide input
on such projects. It applies to all public projects as well as any private projects which require
government approval. CEQA review can take the form of a categorical exemption, a negative
declaration or mitigated negative declaration (ND/MND), or a full environmental impact report
(EIR), depending on a project’s potential effects. CEQA also allows members of the public to
challenge an agency’s approval in court.
Proponents of the Building an Affordable California Act (BACA) contend that the current
process imposes open-ended delay that raises the cost of housing, water, energy, transportation,
health care, and wildfire-resilience projects, and that those costs are ultimately borne by renters,
homebuyers, ratepayers, and taxpayers. The sponsor estimates that permitting and approval
delays add more than $75,000 to the cost of a new single-family home and billions of dollars to
the cost of public infrastructure. Independent research supports the direction of the claim if not
the precise number: an environmental impact report commonly costs from $200,000 to several
million dollars to prepare, industry analyses estimate that regulatory requirements add a wide
range—on the order of several thousand to well over one hundred thousand dollars—to the cost
of a home, and recent academic work on permitting (Soltas and Gruber, 2026) finds that
permitting requirements and delay materially raise housing costs.
Independent empirical study of CEQA litigation provides important context for the measure, and
the pattern has held across more than a decade of data. A Holland & Knight review of every
CEQA lawsuit filed statewide from 2010 through 2012 found that housing, particularly higher-
density infill housing, is the most frequently litigated category of private project, that transit is
the most frequently litigated category of infrastructure, that 49 percent of CEQA lawsuits
targeted taxpayer-funded projects with no private sponsor (parks, schools, libraries, and public
housing), and that roughly two-thirds of petitioners were individuals or local associations, many
without a prior record of environmental advocacy. A more recent study in the same series,
examining litigation filed from 2019 through 2021, found that the housing focus persisted: in
2020 alone, CEQA lawsuits targeted approximately 48,000 approved housing units—close to
half of the roughly 111,000 homes California produces in an average year—with thousands more
units challenged through suits against neighborhood upzoning.
Analysts who view CEQA more favorably draw a different emphasis from overlapping data.
Studies commissioned by the Rose Foundation for Communities and the Environment report that
CEQA lawsuits have averaged roughly 192 per year since 2002 and that only about 1.9 percent
of projects reviewed under CEQA from 2013 through 2021 were litigated, and conclude that
CEQA is not a major obstacle to housing production statewide. Both perspectives bear on this
measure: CEQA litigation is statistically infrequent across the full universe of projects, yet it
falls disproportionately on the housing and taxpayer-funded projects the measure is intended to
accelerate.
SDtaxpayers.org • 3
The measure also arrives against a CEQA baseline that the Legislature changed materially in
2025. Assembly Bill 130 and Senate Bill 131, signed in June 2025, created a broad statutory
CEQA exemption for qualifying infill housing and narrowed review for projects that “near-miss”
an exemption, among other changes. The Building an Affordable California Act is the California
Chamber of Commerce’s response to what proponents view as the limits of those project-specific
fixes: a comprehensive, statewide revision of CEQA procedure rather than additional category-
by-category exemptions. Any comparison of the measure to “current CEQA” in this paper is a
comparison to the post-2025 framework, not to legacy CEQA.
The Proposal
The measure adds a new chapter to the Public Resources Code that applies streamlined CEQA
procedures to a defined set of “essential projects” including housing (single- and multi-family,
senior, student, supportive, farmworker, and commercial-to-residential conversions); health care
facilities; clean drinking water and water-system infrastructure; clean energy generation, storage,
and transmission; education facilities; public safety and wildfire-resilience projects;
transportation; and broadband. The measure does not exempt these projects from CEQA or other
environmental statutes, rather it changes the timeline and the rules of review. Its principal
mechanisms are:
● Application completeness: an agency must determine whether an application is complete
within 30 days, or the application is deemed complete automatically.
● CEQA-track selection: the agency must choose the document type (EIR, ND/MND, or
exemption) within 30 days of completeness.
● Enforceable review timelines: 365 days for an EIR, 180 days for an ND/MND, and 90 days
for an exemption or addendum. If a deadline is missed, the applicant may request a hearing at
which a decision must be made within 60 days, and may seek a writ from the court.
● Final agency decision: the agency must act within 90 days after CEQA review is complete,
and all responsible agencies must act within their own deadlines.
● Narrowed alternatives analysis: an EIR needs to analyze only one feasible alternative
design that reduces environmental impacts plus a “no project” alternative.
● Judicial “shot clock”: courts must resolve a legal challenge within 270 days.
● Standard of review: a court may overturn an approval only where the agency ignored
objective written standards in effect when the application was submitted, and must uphold an
approval supported by substantial evidence—a more deferential standard than the “fair
argument” and “prejudicial abuse of discretion” standards applied under current law.
● Severance (“fix-it ticket”) remedy: where one portion of a review document is found
deficient, only that portion must be corrected and the approval is not rescinded, allowing the
remainder of the project to proceed.
SDtaxpayers.org • 4
● Legal-defense provision: if the Act is challenged in court and both the Governor and
Attorney General decline to defend it, the measure requires the Attorney General to appoint
independent counsel to defend the Act and creates a continuous appropriation from the
General Fund, without regard to fiscal year, to cover that defense.
● Conflicting-measures clause: if another measure concerning the review or approval of
essential projects appears on the same statewide ballot, the two are deemed in conflict, and if
this measure receives more affirmative votes, its provisions prevail in their entirety and the
other measure’s conflicting provisions become null and void. Staff is not aware of a currently
qualified competing measure this clause would apply against.
The sponsor states that the measure preserves local agencies’ authority to approve or deny
projects, retains a public-comment period, strengthens early tribal consultation, and requires
prevailing-wage and skilled-and-trained workforce labor standards.
Fiscal Impact
The measure is not a tax and dedicates no revenue. Its fiscal relevance to taxpayers is indirect but
material: governments are themselves major builders of the essential projects the measure
covers—water systems, roads and bridges, schools, fire stations, and energy infrastructure—and
review delay adds financing, legal, labor, and materials cost to those public projects. The
taxpayer exposure is not merely theoretical. The Holland & Knight litigation study found that
nearly half of all CEQA lawsuits target taxpayer-funded projects with no private sponsor, and
that transit is the most-litigated category of infrastructure; for those projects, the cost of delay
and of defending the litigation falls directly on public budgets. More predictable timelines and a
narrower set of litigable issues would be expected to reduce both the carrying cost and the legal-
defense cost of public capital projects.
The strongest independent support for the measure’s fiscal case comes from the state’s own
analyst. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office, in its December 10, 2025 review,
concluded that the net effect of the measure’s shortened agency and court timelines “likely
result[s] in savings in the longer term,” and noted that faster project completion could increase
state and local tax revenue, such as property tax.
Governance Impact
The Taxpayers Association evaluates not only what a measure costs but how it changes the
structure of public decision-making—who decides, under what standards, with what oversight,
and answerable to whom. In its bond analyses the Association treats governance as a distinct
evaluation axis, examining board policies, oversight committees, and transparency commitments
alongside the financing. This measure is, at its core, a governance measure: it leaves the
SDtaxpayers.org • 5
substantive environmental standards in place and instead rewrites the procedural rules that
allocate authority among agencies, courts, applicants, and the public.
Under CEQA as it operates today, environmental review is enforced largely through private
litigation rather than by a dedicated regulator. Members of the public and organizations may file
suit to compel additional review, and the governing standards are claimant-friendly: for a
negative declaration, the “fair argument” standard requires an agency to prepare a full
environmental impact report whenever any substantial evidence supports a fair argument of a
significant effect—a threshold courts have described as easy to meet. A successful challenge is
typically remedied by a writ that sets aside the approval and requires the agency to redo the
deficient review, and there are no statutory deadlines governing how long agency review or the
ensuing litigation may take. This design gives the public and the courts substantial leverage over
project approvals, which is its intended virtue and, proponents argue, the source of its cost and
delay.
The measure rebalances that structure toward agencies and applicants. It directs courts to review
approvals for substantial evidence rather than under the more searching fair-argument and
independent-judgment standards, which makes a compliant approval harder to overturn. It
restricts the issues that may be litigated to an agency’s departure from objective written standards
in effect when the application was filed, and bars “late” objections not raised during the
comment period. It replaces the set-aside-and-redo remedy with a severance or “fix-it” remedy,
so that a single defective portion of a review document is corrected without rescinding the whole
approval. And it imposes enforceable deadlines on both agencies (365 days for an EIR, 180 for a
negative declaration, 90 for an exemption, and 90 days for a final decision) and courts (270 days
to resolve a challenge). The net effect is a more predictable, schedule-driven process in which
the decisive judgment rests with the permitting agency rather than with a reviewing court or a
litigant.
The accountability the measure adds is real and of a kind the Association generally favors:
objective standards known in advance, firm timelines, and a defined remedy for missed deadlines
replace open-ended, discretionary delay with rules a public can hold agencies to. At the same
time, the measure reduces a different form of accountability—the public’s and the courts’ ability
to force a fuller second look at a project—and concentrates more authority in the approving
agency. This trade is the central governance question the measure poses, and it is distinct from
the 2025 reforms (AB 130 and SB 131), which mostly exempted defined categories of infill
housing from review; this measure instead changes the standards and remedies that apply when
review and litigation do occur, across a far broader set of essential projects.
Proponents
The measure is sponsored by the California Chamber of Commerce through the Committee to
Build an Affordable California. The sponsor reports a coalition of more than 100 organizations,
including business and taxpayer groups (California Business Roundtable, Bay Area Council,
SDtaxpayers.org • 6
numerous regional chambers, and peer taxpayer associations), affordable-housing organizations
(California Council for Affordable Housing, Housing Action Coalition, Leading Builders of
America), clean-energy and water interests (American Clean Power California, California
Energy Storage Alliance, California Water Association), the California Hospital Association,
building and construction trades and contractors, and several civil-rights and community
organizations (CA/HI State Conference NAACP, LULAC). Proponents argue that decades of
project-specific fixes have failed to address the underlying cost of delay and that a
comprehensive, enforceable timeline is needed to lower the cost of housing, energy, water, and
health care while keeping California’s environmental and labor standards in place.
Opponents
Opposition is led by environmental, public-health, and conservation organizations, including
Sierra Club California, Greenbelt Alliance, the Planning and Conservation League, the Center
for Biological Diversity, Communities for a Better Environment, Food & Water Watch, and
Physicians for Social Responsibility–Los Angeles. Opponents argue that the measure weakens
environmental review by compressing timelines and limiting the grounds and remedies for legal
challenges; that the more deferential substantial- evidence standard and the bar on rescinding
approvals make it harder for courts to halt harmful projects; that the costs of pollution and
public-health impacts would shift onto taxpayers and local governments; and that reduced review
could affect air and water quality and communities near industrial projects.
Greenbelt Alliance has published a more detailed critique making several additional points: that
the measure’s definition of “essential projects” is broad enough to cover freeways, freeway
expansions, and large-scale sprawl development rather than only the infill housing the sponsor
emphasizes; that compressing review to fixed timelines is unworkable for large projects
requiring extensive species and habitat surveys; that limiting the alternatives analysis to the
applicant’s own design plus a “no project” option removes a tool historically used to redirect
development away from sensitive land; and that the measure may be cheaper to build under but
more costly to sustain over time, given the long-run infrastructure and maintenance costs
associated with sprawl. Staff independently reviewed Greenbelt’s additional claim that the
measure imposes a two-thirds legislative-supermajority requirement on future amendment and
found no such provision in the qualified initiative text; the measure contains no amendment
section at all, meaning the default rule under Article II, Section 10(c) of the California
Constitution would apply instead, under which the Legislature may not amend or repeal the Act
without a subsequent vote of the people unless the Act itself provides otherwise.

Interesting — the SD Taxpayers Association analysis (which supports Prop 45) claims "Staff independently reviewed Greenbelt's additional claim that the measure imposes a two-thirds legislative-supermajority requirement on future amendment and found no such provision in the qualified initiative text; the measure contains no amendment section at all." But I read the final ballot text and Section 21034 "Amendments" DOES exist: "The Legislature may amend this chapter by a statute passed in each house of the Legislature by rollcall vote entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership concurring, provided that the statute is consistent with, and furthers the purposes of, this chapter."

So the SD Taxpayers analysis was based on the pre-qualification initiative text (Aug 2026, maybe an earlier version), and is factually wrong on that point relative to the final text in the voter guide. That's an important correction — the two-thirds amendment lock-in IS in the final text (Section 21034, Article 8). Good thing I read the actual text.

Also the SD Taxpayers doc says the LAO concluded long-term net savings — but the final VIG analysis says "Uncertain, potentially more significant positive or negative longer-term fiscal effects" and initial costs high tens of millions to >$100M annually. The Dec 2025 LAO review at qualification said likely net savings long-term, but the official VIG analysis says uncertain. I'll use the official VIG language.

Let me verify Section 21034 is in the final text — yes, I read it: "21034. Amendments — The Legislature may amend this chapter by a statute passed in each house of the Legislature by rollcall vote entered in the journal, two-thirds of the membership concurring, provided that the statute is consistent with, and furthers the purposes of, this chapter."

Great. So the lock-in critique is accurate for the final text.

Now I have a comprehensive picture. Let me summarize the decision framework:

**Arguments for YES:**
1. CEQA delay/abuse is real: Holland & Knight study of 498 appellate decisions 2013-2023 — housing is top target (25.5%), 64% of challenged projects were infill, litigation typically takes ~5 years, agencies win 75% but projects stall/lose financing. Real costs.
2. Hard deadlines (365 business days EIR, 180 ND/MND, 90 exemption), one-shot completeness corrections list, 30-day deemed-complete, 270-day judicial shot clock, "fix-it" remedy rather than project-killing set-aside.
3. Doesn't repeal CEQA or substantive environmental laws (Clean Air/Water Act, ESA, Coastal Act remain); doesn't exempt any project from review; agencies retain approval/denial authority.
4. Preserves (mostly) labor standards (Section 21183.5 prevailing wage/skilled workforce for non-housing essential projects; housing over 85 ft).
5. Broad support: 28 newspaper editorial boards, CalChamber, CBIA, hospitals, water associations, affordable housing groups (CCAC, Housing Action Coalition), NAACP CA, LULAC, CA Taxpayers Association, Bay Area Council, clean energy groups.
6. Potential long-run savings; LAO notes faster public project delivery lowers costs, more projects → more tax revenue.
7. Excludes the most controversial: jails, new oil/gas production, Delta conveyance, high-speed rail, nuclear.

**Arguments for NO:**
1. **Judicial review gutted**: Claims limited to "objective existing laws" (uniformly verifiable written benchmarks knowable before application). CEQA's core — whether an impact is "significant," mitigation adequacy, alternatives — is judgment-based. Courts may not rescind approval; remedy limited to halting only the noncomplying part; injunctions require **clear and convincing evidence** of a **specific adverse public safety impact** — not environmental harm. Post-approval, later implementation/subsequent approvals can't be challenged at all; minor modifications can't be challenged. This is the "paper tiger" critique from Stanford's Sivas, and it's textually accurate.
2. **Freeze/vesting**: Impacts judged under laws & standards in place when application submitted ("existing laws"), and cross-references frozen to Dec 31, 2025 statutes regardless of later amendment/repeal. Enables strategic early filing to lock in weaker standards; undermines the state's ability to update protections (Biber's key critique).
3. **One applicant-designed alternative**, presumed to lessen impacts, and agencies barred from requiring any others. Removes the central tool for steering development away from sensitive land.

Boswell, Watson Land), utilities (PG&E $2.9M, Edison $2M, Sempra $1M), CA Resources Corp, Prologis (data centers/warehouses), Bloom Energy, AT&T.
